Gonzaga.title: Denver Nuggets sign former Gonzaga point guard Ryan Nembhard to two-way contract
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Gonzaga point guard Ryan Nembhard is on the move for the third time this offseason.

Nembhard, who was traded from the Dallas Mavericks to the Atlanta Hawks on July 19 before being shipped to the Charlotte Hornets last week, has seemingly found a permanent landing spot for the 2026-27 season after signing a two-way contract with the Denver Nuggets.

The second-year pro will team up with former Gonzaga wing Julian Strawther in Denver and split time between the NBA’s Nuggets and G League Grand Rapids Gold in Grand Rapids, Michigan. Denver waived guard KJ Simpson to open up a two-way spot for Nembhard.

It becomes the fourth team for Nembhard since a two-game stint with the Mavericks this July at NBA Summer League in Las Vegas. Days after his second Summer League game, Nembhard was involved in a three-team trade that sent the former Zag to Atlanta in exchange for Zaccharie Risacher. The Hawks also acquired Oklahoma City guard Lu Dort as part of the deal.

Nembhard’s time with Atlanta lasted just two months before the Hawks traded the point guard, Buddy Hield and cash considerations to Charlotte for forward Dorian Finney-Smith. Within days of that move, reports indicated that Charlotte intended to waive Nembhard before training camp, making him an unrestricted free agent.

The Mavericks signed Nembhard to an undrafted two-way deal last summer and leaned on the point guard throughout the regular season. Nembhard’s two-way contract was converted to a standard deal late in the season and the rookie made 60 appearances for Dallas, including 27 starts.

Nembhard, who broke Gonzaga’s single-season assists record in each of his two seasons with the program, averaged 6.6 points, 5.3 assists and 2.2 rebounds for the Mavericks while shooting 41.5% from the field, 35.6% from the 3-point line and 80.6% from the free throw line.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga unveils full 2026-27 schedule, will open Pac-12 season with rivalry matchup at WSU
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s inaugural Pac-12 season is right around the corner and might feel even closer now that the Bulldogs have a full regular-season schedule to parse through.

The Pac-12 Conference revealed its men’s basketball schedule on Wednesday, allowing Gonzaga to formally announce its complete 31-game regular-season slate featuring at least 15 nonconference games and 16 more as part of the Pac-12’s double round-robin format.

There weren’t any new developments with Gonzaga’s nonleague slate, which has been pieced together over the last handful of months and includes at least 10 games against high-major opponents. The Zags could potentially play an 11th power-conference foe, and 16th nonconference game, if they qualify for the championship game at the Players Era Festival in Las Vegas.

Gonzaga will have to get through a new batch of opponents to win its first Pac-12 championship, but Mark Few’s team will open conference play against a familiar foe when it travels to Pullman on Jan. 6 for the 155th all-time meeting with Washington State.

The conference home opener is scheduled for Jan. 9 against Colorado State, followed by a Jan. 13 road test at Fresno State.

Gonzaga returns home on Jan. 16 for one of its most-anticipated matchups in the new Pac-12, pitting Few against Boise State and longtime Zags assistant Leon Rice. The game also doubles as a reunion for the Few family with AJ Few, the oldest son of Gonzaga’s Hall of Fame coach, entering his second season on Boise State’s staff as a director of player personnel.

After the Boise State matchup, Gonzaga will be back on the road for a two-game swing against Utah State (Jan. 21) and Oregon State (Jan. 24). The Aggies are targeting a fifth straight NCAA Tournament appearance under their fourth different coach and announced a sellout for the Gonzaga game two weeks before the schedule was released.

Three days later, the Zags will face another first-year coach, Oregon State’s Justin Joyner, in Corvallis, Oregon. Joyner was an assistant coach for Michigan’s national title-winning team last season and had the scouting report when the Wolverines thumped Gonzaga 101-61 in the Players Era championship.

Gonzaga won’t leave the state of Washington for its next three games, hosting Fresno State on Jan. 27 before traveling to Seattle on Jan. 30 for a nonleague matchup with Oregon at Climate Pledge Arena. The Zags return home on Feb. 4 for their first-ever meeting with Texas State, which left the Sun Belt Conference to join the revamped Pac-12.

Two more intriguing road games follow for Gonzaga, which travels to play San Diego State at Viejas Arena before a return game with Boise State on Feb. 10 at ExtraMile Arena.

The Zags travel back to Spokane for a single game against Washington State on Feb. 17 before leaving for another nonconference game on Feb. 20 against Duke at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit.

Gonzaga will stay on the road to play Texas State in San Marcos on Feb. 25 before returning to the Inland Northwest for a two-game home swing against San Diego State (Feb. 27) and Oregon State (March 3). The team’s Pac-12 regular-season finale will take place on March 6 at Colorado State.

The Pac-12 Tournament opens just three days later at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas, but Gonzaga could avoid playing on March 9, 10 or 11 if the Zags are able to secure a No. 1 or 2 seed and earn a bye to the Pac-12 semifinals on March 12. The conference championship game will take place on March 13 and air on CBS/Paramount+.

Tipoff times and television broadcast details for the majority of Gonzaga’s nonconference games, and all 16 conference games, will be announced in the coming weeks.

Under the new Pac-12 schedule, all nine teams are playing 16 games, with home and road matchups against each of the other eight schools. No team is playing three consecutive road games or four of five games on the road and every team is opening and closing its conference schedule with one home and road game across its first and final two contests.

Zags add exhibition

Gonzaga’s preseason exhibition schedule will start on Oct. 24 against Arkansas and resume four days later with a home matchup against NAIA opponent Lewis-Clark State.

A tipoff time and television details for the Oct. 28 exhibition have yet to be announced.

The Lewiston-based school has been a common exhibition opponent for Gonzaga, with the Zags and Warriors meeting as recently as 2023-24, when Graham Ike scored 24 points and Braden Huff added 21 to help Few’s team pull away for a 96-58 win.

Ferris High School product Dylan Skaife returns to LCSC’s roster after starting in all 32 games for the Warriors as a sophomore.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga Men’s Basketball, Altana Announce Jersey Patch Partnership
Gonzaga.summary: SPOKANE, Wash. – Gonzaga University and Gonzaga Men's Basketball have announced Altana, the world's first AI network for global trade, as the program's official jersey patch partner for the 2026-27 season.

Gonzaga.title: Wait continues for Gonzaga's Xaivian Lee, Ines Bettencourt after California injunction hearing
Gonzaga.summary:
A preliminary injunction hearing held Tuesday afternoon in Santa Clara County came with some good news, some bad news and, in many ways, no news at all for a pair of Gonzaga players seeking a fifth year of college eligibility.

The Glancey v. NCAA lawsuit including Xaivian Lee, a Florida transfer looking to extend his career with Mark Few and the Gonzaga men, and Ines Bettencourt, a returning starter hoping to return for one final season with Lisa Fortier and the Zag women, continued Tuesday afternoon in Northern California, where a Santa Clara County judge heard statements from player plaintiffs and coaches, along with arguments from attorneys representing the NCAA.

Lee, Bettencourt and more than 70 other player plaintiffs involved in the case are seeking a preliminary injunction that would grant them a fifth year of eligibility, extending their clocks months after the NCAA passed its new 5-in-5 eligibility model.

No ruling was made Tuesday and another hearing was scheduled for Oct. 20, according to Ryan Downton, one of the attorneys representing the player plaintiffs.

“There was not enough time for all of the players and coaches to testify today, so the hearing will resume on October 20,” Downton wrote in an email to The Spokesman-Review. “The TRO (temporary restraining order) remains in place pending the next hearing.”

Tuesday’s no-decision could be interpreted as either a negative or positive development.

Although players now have to wait at least three weeks for clarity, the TRO issued by the Superior Court of Santa Clara on Aug. 7 gives them eligibility until a judge makes a final ruling. Specifically, it allows Lee and Bettencourt to practice with their respective teams and participate in the upcoming Kraziness in the Kennel and Numerica Fan Fest events scheduled the next two weekends.

The second injunction hearing will take place four days before the Gonzaga men travel to Fayetteville, Arkansas, for a preseason exhibition against Arkansas and seven days before the Zag women host Westmont College for their only preseason exhibition on Oct. 27.

A preliminary injunction would signify an important step for Lee and Bettencourt, but the NCAA is expected to counter with an appeal and push for a stay motion, which would reverse both players’ eligibility until the case is heard by a Court of Appeals.

Two other incoming Gonzaga men’s basketball transfers seeking a fifth year of eligibility, Javon Bennett (Dayton) and Chauncey Wiggins (Florida State), initially secured eligibility through similar injunctions in Ohio and Georgia, but judges in both cases granted the NCAA’s request for a stay, making both players ineligible for the time being.

Downton is representing player plaintiffs in a handful of other 5-in-5 cases across the country, including the Ohio lawsuit involving Bennett and Georgia lawsuit involving Wiggins. It’s possible final verdicts on one or multiple cases won’t arrive before Gonzaga opens the season on Nov. 2 against Purdue in Las Vegas.

A handful of fifth-year hopefuls including BYU’s Jaxon Kohler, a Michigan State transfer, testified in person Tuesday afternoon. St. John’s coach Rick Pitino also attended the injunction hearing in Santa Clara to testify. Reed Bailey, a fifth-year forward who transferred from Indiana to St. John’s this offseason, is one of the player plaintiffs named in the lawsuit.

“The NCAA should give up on all of these lawsuits and let everyone in the Class of 2022 play this year,” Pitino said during the hearing, according to a post on X from Downton’s firm, the Texas Trial Group.

Other notable players named in the California suit include former UCLA guards Donovan Dent and Skyy Clark, both of whom transferred to play for LSU and first-year coach Will Wade. If granted an injunction, all three of Lee, Dent and Clark could be on the floor when the Tigers travel to Spokane for a Nov. 14 matchup with Gonzaga at Numerica Veterans Arena.

Former Saint Mary’s, UConn and UC Santa Barbara guard Aidan Mahaney is also part of the lawsuit, as is fifth-year point guard Moe Odum, who faced the Zags at each of his three college stops: Pacific, Pepperdine and Arizona State.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga announces jersey patch sponsorship with AI network Altana
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga will be debuting not one but two new patches on its men’s basketball jerseys in 2026-27.

Along with the Pac-12 Conference logo, Gonzaga players will wear a patch to represent the school’s newly announced partnership with Altana, an artificial intelligence network for supply chain management and trade commerce.

Gonzaga and other college programs around the country are taking advantage of jersey sponsorships as new revenue streams after receiving approval from the NCAA in January. As of Aug. 1, Division I teams can use up to two patches of no more than 4 square inches for regular-season games.

“Altana is an exceptional organization that represents innovation and forward thinking, and we are excited to welcome them as a partner of Gonzaga Athletics and Gonzaga Basketball,” Gonzaga Athletic Director Chris Standiford said in a school news release. “As we enter a new era for Gonzaga Athletics and begin competition in the Pac-12, we are grateful for Altana’s support and belief in our student-athletes and our program. We look forward to building a strong partnership together.”

Altana, founded in 2018 by Evan Smith, Peter Swartz and Raphael Tehranian and based in New York City, claims to be the world’s first AI network for global trade. The company uses AI to suggest efficient trade routes when considering factors like tariffs and regulations on forced labor, for example, according to its website.

The fast-growing company contracts with retailers shipping product across the globe. It uses AI models fed with public and private data to track each step a product takes in the global supply chain, sometimes down to its raw materials.

The company has notable partnerships with government agencies such as the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, as well as retailers.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection has contracted with Altana since 2023, using their global supply chain map, or “Atlas,” to help prevent products made with forced labor from entering the United States, according to a news release from Altana at the time of their contract.

“We’re excited to have Altana represented on our jerseys this season,” Gonzaga coach Mark Few said in the Gonzaga news release. “They’re an incredibly innovative and successful company, and we appreciate their support of Gonzaga Basketball and our student-athletes. It’s an exciting time for our program, and we’re looking forward to representing Altana on the court.”

Gonzaga becomes the second local Division I school to reach a jersey patch sponsorship in recent months. In June, Washington State announced a five-year, $8.43 million agreement with Colville Tribes to wear the company’s patch on all of its athletic uniforms.

Gonzaga.title: Experienced Gonzaga women return Ines Bettencourt after court ruling: 'It's a new energy'
Gonzaga.summary:
Expectations are going to be high for the Gonzaga women’s basketball team in 2026-27.

A late addition to the roster now may blow those expectations through the roof of McCarthey Athletic Center.

The Zags were set to essentially return their entire team from 2025-26 with the exception of guard Ines Bettencourt, who graduated last spring.

The NCAA’s new five-years-to-play-five-seasons eligibility model announced this summer opened the door for the Portugal native to fight for an additional year of eligibility. She joined a California class action lawsuit, gaining a temporary restraining order and immediate eligibility.

Bettencourt returned to Spokane on Sept. 5.

Now the band is back together for Gonzaga, which will have one of the deepest rosters in the nation with 10 returners, including five starters to go with two transfers and one freshman.

Bettencourt and GU coach Lisa Fortier were cautious in calling it a done deal when the Zags took the court for their first preseason practice last week. A preliminary hearing on Tuesday in Santa Clara County appeared to push a final decision to October 20, at the earliest. 

The Zags are proceeding as if they’ll have Bettencourt.

“It’s been a long summer ever since I graduated,” said Bettencourt, who went back to Portugal and practiced frequently with her national team. “I kind of knew that this would be a possibility. So I was just working behind the scenes and talking with Lisa (Fortier), not really telling anyone else because it wasn’t for sure.”

As soon as the NCAA adopted the new eligibility format, Bettencourt began talking to Fortier and Gonzaga compliance officials “to figure out what exactly I have to do to come back because as an international it’s harder to come back than an American.”

There Bettencourt was going through drills and running up and down the court with her teammates like she had never left.

“Like McKynnlie (Dalan, senior forward) said, ‘we set you off, (had) all these goodbyes and now you’re back.’ ”

Fortier said Gonzaga will proceed as if Bettencourt will be eligible the whole season.

“She had asked us pretty early on in April or May (about coming back) and she was kind of joking at first,” Fortier said. “No one actually thought that any of this was gonna happen. The answer was like sure (you can come back).”

Bettencourt is stoked to have another year with her coaches and what she calls her “best friends.”

“Just having one more shot at this, making the (NCAA) Tournament. Just being more prepared for whatever’s next for me,” Bettencourt said. “So it’s just awesome. Everyone was happy for me.”

Fortier is overjoyed to have Bettencourt back – something the Zags never thought would be an option four months ago.

“She’s one of ours so we would love to have her back,” Fortier said. “She shows up every day around the program and she takes care of business like a professional. She’s a pro in all ways.”

The familiarity will be a team strength no doubt.

“We know each other,” Bettencourt said. “So it was just super nice for them to receive me well again.”

Bettencourt spent most of the summer playing 3-on-3 in Portugal. It was different preparation for returning to Gonzaga.

“I have to run more now,” Bettencourt said, smiling.

Bettencourt took over a leadership role last year as the team’s lone senior. Now as a graduate, she wants to continue to lean into leadership.

“Just building on the leadership,” she said.

She expects to be a better player, too.

“Stay composed and stay consistent at everything,” she said about her personal expectations. “I’m just taking it day by day because I get to come back and be with my teammates, with my coaches, and practice with them again.”

Junior point guard Allie Turner started alongside Bettencourt in the backcourt last year. Turner, Bettencourt and sophomore forward Lauren Whittaker all lived together last year.

The trio can’t run that arrangement back as living assignments had already been passed out. But Turner is glad to have Bettencourt along for one more year.

“We’re super happy to have her back,” Turner said. “It’s a new energy.”

Whittaker agreed.

“For a long time we didn’t really think it was an option. And then kind of a quick turnaround within a couple of weeks we heard (she) was coming back,” Whittaker said. “She’s a player that I think is really seamless to bring back to the team. She has a lot of experience and was a great leader last year and obviously a great player. So it was kind of just an easy transition for her and everyone has been really supportive of it. It’s kind of like she’s never left.”

Bettencourt is looking forward to returning to McCarthey Athletic Center and seeing the fans for FanFest on Oct. 10.

“Super excited,” Bettencourt said. “I’m sure they (the fans) are going to be like ‘what? What are you doing here again?’ But I’m super excited to be back in front of all the fans with my team and showing them again what we can bring this year.”

Gonzaga.title: Who is 2027 Gonzaga commit Dooney Johnson?
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – It wouldn’t have been apparent that Dooney Johnson was dealing with any kind of physical stress last spring when the five-star Gonzaga commit carried Milwaukee Juneau to the school’s first state championship.

Not when he exploded for 40 points, accounting for 61% of his team’s overall scoring production during a third-round victory against Living Word Lutheran.

Not a week later when he popped Howard Grove High School for 36 points, 12 rebounds and five assists in the state quarterfinals.

Certainly not during a championship matchup against Cambridge, when Johnson rattled off 14 consecutive first-half points – and 23 in the game, with seven rebounds – to help Milwaukee Juneau rally back from a first-quarter deficit, win 62-54 and complete a 28-1 season.

There were no obvious signs of discomfort, just dominance from someone who averaged 27.8 points, 8.5 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 3.4 steals for a Milwaukee Juneau team that won 27 straight games to finish No. 8 in MaxPreps’ postseason national Top 25 rankings.

Only a few people in Johnson’s close circle knew about the underlying issue he was facing as he guided the Pioneers to a historic season.

“We never really put it out there, he won a state title on basically a fractured ankle,” said Johnson’s father Torre, also the head coach at Milwaukee Juneau last season. “Once the state tournament was over, we sat out for a whole month.”

It’s a window into the competitive drive and winning mindset Gonzaga’s first high school commit in the class of 2027 commit plans to bring to Spokane next fall, after one more prep season at East River High in Orlando, Florida – the school Johnson announced he’d be transferring to last month.

“I never really sit out during injuries, especially I can still go out there and somewhat play, especially to my full potential,” Dooney told The Spokesman-Review in July while competing for AAU Team Herro at a Nike EYBL (Elite Youth Basketball League) event in Las Vegas. “I always want to be out there for myself, not even just myself but for my team because I know I can push through it and continue to be there and compete at the highest level.”

• • • 

Thirteen years ago, Torre Johnson coached the Wisconsin-based Playground Elite AAU program to a 10-and-under national championship in Cocoa Beach, Florida.

It’s nearly impossible to identify Division I talent at a phase when players are still trying to grasp the game’s fundamentals, but one of Johnson’s fifth-graders was athletically advanced for his age and already a step or two ahead of his peers.

A basketball-obsessed toddler, Dooney took advantage of every opportunity to tag along to his father’s AAU games and practices. Although Dooney can’t remember his actual introduction to Jalen Suggs, the Gonzaga commit maintained a close relationship to the former Gonzaga guard and father Larry through basketball, and Jalen eventually became a key mentor to the now five-star prospect.

“Literally just a young fella running around the gym,” Suggs said, looking back at his first memories of Dooney. “Always at all the games, always had a rock in his hands and his dad was amazing. Always showed me the utmost love and really helped me on the mental side of everything as far as handling games, handling pressure, staying locked in and making sure I’m attacking every weekend we have.

“It’s gone right into Dooney. You see he applies that every game he plays. Super competitor. So for me, it’s just dope seeing him grow from that little kid to now he’s doing his thing and even coming into the Zags, it’s such a full journey. Very full circle.”

Now in his sixth season with the Orlando Magic, Suggs offered support to Johnson through the college recruiting process and not surprisingly, gave a strong endorsement for the Zags, who went to the national championship in 2021 after the guard’s iconic Final Four buzzer-beater against UCLA.

“They’re my guys,” Dooney said of Jalen and Larry Suggs. “But it was overall just the school and the coaches, how they treated me.”

Gonzaga’s playing style and culture were two of the main factors that prompted an early commitment from the Milwaukee native, who collected 11 other high-major offers before his junior high school season.

“It was a real nice time going there, everyone was nice, brotherhood, the campus was great,” Johnson said. “It was just an all-around brotherhood, it felt good. … Fast-paced system, really can just be who you are on the floor. Not too many sets, just be who you are and go get a bucket.”

Suggs and Johnson, the two highest-rated guard commits in Gonzaga history according to 247Sports.com, reconnected this summer. Suggs pulled double duty in Las Vegas, following Orlando’s NBA Summer League team at the Thomas & Mack Center while making time to watch Johnson and Team Herro at Nike EYBL a few miles away at the Vegas Convention Center.

Gonzaga assistants Brian Michaelson and Zach Norvell Jr. also traded days in Vegas, catching each of Johnson’s four games at the EYBL tournament.

“We were always pushing the Zags,” Suggs said. “It’s a beautiful place to be, you’re going to play great basketball, they’re going to really win and really treat you like family. That was just another piece. They really want you for the human you are and that’s really what we were trying to preach to him and understanding he can go anywhere and all these schools around the country, all the money, all the names and everything, notoriety, but there’s no place like Gonzaga, there’s no place like Spokane in the country in my opinion.

“I’m glad he kind of took that. B-Mike and Few did their job showing him the love. I can’t wait to see him in Spokane.”

• • • 

Johnson sat idle for a month after celebrating with teammates and lifting the state title on his fractured ankle at the University of Wisconsin’s Kohl Center. With highly-competitive Nike EYBL games approaching, Torre urged his son to take a few more weeks off, fearing the risk of re-injury.

Those efforts proved unsuccessful.

“When I asked him to sit out that first EYBL session until he gets his rhythm back, he looked me in my eyes and said, ‘What , Dad, you don’t think I’m going to be able to compete?’ ” Torre recalled. “So at the end of the day like I tell him, he’s the engine, I’m just the driver.”

Even in a slightly limited capacity, Johnson made his impact on the EYBL circuit, leading Team Herro – the AAU program sponsored by Milwaukee Bucks guard Tyler Herro – to an 18-4 record and semifinal run at the prestigious Peach Jam event based in Augusta, Georgia. The 6-foot-5 Johnson paced Team Herro at 14.9 ppg during the AAU circuit to go with 4.4 rpg, 3.0 apg and 1.1 spg.

Entering the AAU season, Johnson was mostly concentrated on making defensive strides, vowing to hold the opponent’s “star players or second star players” below their scoring averages and “continue to be a defensive anchor for my team.”

Chris Herro, Tyler’s father and the coach of Johnson’s 17U Team Herro squad, noticed growth there and in other areas.

“He’s really become a leader more,” Herro said. “He hit some big shots there for us and you’re getting a dog at the end of the day. He’s going to push them to the next level of competitiveness, which I don’t think Gonzaga’s had in a while. They haven’t had that in a while, that competitive edge. It’s good, I think he’s going to learn from coach Few.”

Johnson’s distribution and willingness to get teammates involved were other bright spots, particularly coming off a high school season where the guard often needed to score at a high clip for his team to have success.

The No. 27 prospect in the country, Johnson wasn’t the highest-rated player on his AAU squad, playing alongside Duke commit Kager Knueppel, the 17th-rated player in the country and younger brother of Charlotte Hornets guard Kon Knueppel. Team Herro’s roster also consisted of Iowa State commits Donovan Davis and Jack Konen, Nebraska commit Ty Schlagel and top-100 prospect Deuce McDuffie.

“He’s grown a lot in the realm of being able to play with other really good players, because that’s part of it,” Chris Herro said. “When you go out of high school, you’ve got to be able to play with other guys and that’s where he’s grown. He’s sharing the ball more, he understands that part of it, so yeah he’s doing well.”

The Zags are still a year away from deciding how they’ll deploy Johnson, who should be a candidate to get rotation minutes as a freshman, or potentially vie for a starting role for a program that could lose three point guards from the 2026-27 roster.

The consensus from AAU teammates and coaches is that Johnson is a hybrid point guard – someone who can create for himself and hunt shots as needed or fill more of a pass-first role when the situation calls for it.

“I’d say about 50/50,” said Davis, a four-star power forward who had recruiting conversations with Gonzaga before committing to Iowa State. “He’s really good at scoring. That’s the thing he’s really known for.”

Johnson’s big frame, skill level, athleticism and versatility will probably evoke one or two comparisons to the former Gonzaga guard he’s leaned on for advice and mentorship.

“So versatile, man,” Suggs said of Johnson. “Few’s going to love him in that sense because he can come out here and do everything. He can defend the best player, he’s coming out getting guys involved, he’s a force going downhill; the rim and his jumper and his skill are going to continue to evolve so I think he’s in a great space right now.”

• • • 

As a rising prospect who climbed to No. 21 in On3.com’s national rankings this summer, Johnson’s managing a busy schedule as he prepares for his final go-round with high school basketball.

Just consider his summer calendar. In addition to Nike EYBL stops in Atlanta, Memphis, Kansas City, Las Vegas and Augusta, Johnson traveled to the Pangos All-American Camp in Vegas, the NBPA Top 100 Camp in Rock Hill, South Carolina, the Chris Paul Elite Guard Camp in Vegas, the Nike Academy in Thousand Oaks, California, and the Nike NYvsNY game in New York City.

Shortly after his move to Florida, Johnson was invited to take part in the USA Basketball Junior National Minicamp from Oct. 9-11 in Colorado Springs, Colorado. A full high school schedule and All-American games in the spring are likely to follow.

Johnson has plenty on his plate and even more on his calendar before he can pack his things, move to the Inland Northwest and don a Gonzaga uniform for the first time, but judging by conversations with the guard and volume of Zag-centric posts on his Instagram account, that day also can’t arrive soon enough.

“Just got to be patient, but I’m always ready to go be at Gonzaga,” he said. “Great program, great coaches. Especially coach Few, he was really great when I went there. B-Mike, that’s my guy. So yeah it’s going to be good.”

Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga standout Drew Timme signs training camp deal with Minnesota Timberwolves
Gonzaga.summary:
Drew Timme will join the Minnesota Timberwolves for training camp with hopes of latching on to the team’s regular-season roster.

After spending the 2025-26 season on a two-way contract with the Los Angeles Lakers, Gonzaga’s career scoring leader signed a training camp deal with the Timberwolves on Friday, Michael Scotto of HoopsHype.com reported.

Timme played in 27 games for the Lakers last season, making one start while averaging 3.4 points, 1.2 rebounds and 0.9 assists. He appeared in 24 more games for the G League South Bay Lakers, averaging 23.7 ppg, 8.5 rpg and 4.9 apg during the regular season playing alongside former Gonzaga frontcourt mate Anton Watson. Timme’s production in the G League landed him a spot on the All-NBA G League second team.

The Lakers declined to tender a qualifying offer to Timme this offseason, making the former Gonzaga standout a free agent, and the forward elected not to participate in NBA Summer League for the first time after spending the last three summers with the Milwaukee Bucks, Sacramento Kings and Lakers.

Timme made his NBA debut in 2024-25 with the Brooklyn Nets, averaging 12.1 ppg, 7.2 rpg and 2.2 apg during a nine-game stretch to close the regular season.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga Adds French Guard Nathan De Sousa
Gonzaga.summary: SPOKANE, Wash. – Gonzaga men's basketball head coach Mark Few announced the addition of Nathan De Sousa, an experienced guard from France, for the 2026-27 season.

Gonzaga.title: Tipoff time set for nonconference matchup between Gonzaga, Duke
Gonzaga.summary:
One of the most anticipated matchups on Gonzaga’s nonconference schedule now has an official start time.

Gonzaga and Duke will tip off at 5 p.m. on Feb. 20 when two teams expected to start the season ranked inside the Top 25 meet at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit.

The nonconference game will air exclusively on Amazon Prime as part of Duke’s multiyear contract with the popular streaming service. Information on how to purchase tickets will be announced at a later date.

Duke is playing two other Amazon Prime games this season, matching up with UConn on Nov. 25 at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas and Texas Tech on Dec. 21 at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

It will be the sixth all-time meeting between the Zags and Blue Devils and first game since Nov. 26, 2021, when Paolo Banchero and Duke held off Chet Holmgren and Gonzaga in a matchup between the players eventually selected No. 1 and 2 in the NBA draft.

Gonzaga’s most recent win in the series came in the championship of the 2018 Maui Invitational, when Rui Hachimura and Brandon Clarke helped guide Mark Few’s team to an 89-87 victory over a top-ranked Duke team led by Zion Williamson, R.J. Barrett and Cam Reddish.

The Blue Devils won each of the three prior meetings, picking up a 66-52 victory during the 2015 NCAA Elite Eight at NRG Stadium in Houston and claiming nonconference wins at Madison Square Garden in 2007 and 2010.

Both teams could open the 2026-27 season inside the top 10 or 15 in preseason national rankings, with Duke appearing as high as No. 2 in a few early polls.

The Blue Devils will have to replace the Naismith Player of the Year for the second straight season after losing center Cam Boozer to the NBA, but return four of their top six scorers from a year ago and add high-scoring Wisconsin transfer John Blackwell. Additionally, Duke welcomes a quartet of five-star prospects, headlined by FC Barcelona product Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje.

Gonzaga.title: French point guard Nathan De Sousa secures NCAA eligibility, officially joins Gonzaga's roster
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s roster is still under construction less than two months out from the season opener against Purdue, but Mark Few and his coaching staff can breathe a bit easier after receiving some clarity at the point guard position earlier this week.

Nathan De Sousa, a 23-year-old native of France who committed to Gonzaga in June, signed a financial aid agreement with the school on Thursday, two days after the NCAA cleared the point guard to compete in 2026-27.

It guarantees the Zags will carry at least one point guard on their roster this fall after months of uncertainty stemming from Jack Kayil’s unexpected decision to stay in the NBA draft and Mario Saint-Supery’s shocking departure to Valencia in mid-July.

According to Bebasket France, De Sousa received the “green light” from the NCAA on Tuesday after waiting roughly three months to learn if he’d be able to suit up for the Zags this season. It’s expected he’ll have one season of eligibility with the Zags.

Gonzaga formally announced De Sousa’s addition on Thursday morning through a news release and social media photos/videos depicting the guard in a No. 7 practice jersey at McCarthey Athletic Center.

De Sousa brings extensive professional experience to Spokane after spending four of the last five seasons with Cholet of France’s premier LNB Elite league. The point guard averaged 10.9 points, 4.9 assists and 2.5 rebounds last season while appearing in 36 LNB Elite contests.

He made 43.4% of his shots from the field and drastically improved his outside shooting, making 36.1% after connecting on just 18.8% of his 3s the year before.

De Sousa started in Cholet’s backcourt alongside Gerald Ayayi, the older brother of former Gonzaga standout Joel Ayayi. He’ll be one of two French natives on the team’s roster this fall, alongside freshman wing Juwan Ekanga-Ehawa, who signed with the Zags on June 20. They join an impressive list of French players to come through Gonzaga’s program that includes Ayayi, Killian Tillie, Ronny Turiaf and others.

The Zags could have two more point guards signed by the time they open the season on Nov. 2 against Purdue. Florida transfer Xaivian Lee and Dayton transfer Javon Bennett committed to GU last month, but both are still waiting on lawsuits to know if they’ll be eligible for a fifth college season.

Lee is eligible at the moment through a temporary restraining order granted to the point guard and other players in California, but the NCAA is expected to appeal and attempt to overturn the decision in the coming weeks.

After initially earning a fifth season of eligibility through a preliminary injunction in Ohio, Bennett is ineligible for the time being after the court granted the NCAA’s stay request, temporarily reversing the decision. A Court of Appeals in Ohio heard oral arguments from the NCAA and plaintiffs earlier this week and is expected to make a final ruling on the case soon.

Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga point guard Ryan Nembhard traded to Charlotte Hornets
Gonzaga.summary:
Roughly two months after landing Ryan Nembhard from the Dallas Mavericks in a three-team trade, the Atlanta Hawks are sending the former Gonzaga point guard to the Charlotte Hornets.

Nembhard was one of three players involved in a trade on Tuesday that sent the second-year point guard, Buddy Hield and cash considerations to the Hornets in exchange for forward Dorian Finney-Smith.

An undrafted rookie who started in 27 of 60 games for the Mavericks last season, Nembhard was traded to Atlanta in July. The Hawks acquired Nembhard and Oklahoma City guard Lu Dort in a transaction that sent Atlanta’s Zaccharie Risacher and a protected future second-round pick to Dallas, two future second-round picks to Oklahoma City and one second-round pick from Dallas to Oklahoma City.

Nembhard posted solid numbers as a rookie, averaging 6.6 points to go along with 5.3 assists and just 1.4 turnovers in 19.5 minutes per game. He made 41.5% of his shots from the field and 35.6% of his looks from the 3-point line.

After Charlotte traded All-Star guard LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves this offseason, 26-year-old Coby White is expected to assume starting point guard duties for the Hornets in 2026-27, although he could face stiff competition from Nembhard, veteran Dennis Schroeder and rookie Christian Anderson.

Gonzaga.title: Report: Toronto Raptors sign former Gonzaga guard Malachi Smith to two-way deal
Gonzaga.summary:
After making 15 appearances for the Brooklyn Nets toward the end of the regular season, former Gonzaga guard Malachi Smith will have another opportunity to contribute for an Eastern Conference franchise in 2026-27.

The Toronto Raptors converted Smith to a two-way contract on Monday, according to Michael Scotto. The move was possible after the team upgraded rookie guard Jaden Bradley to a standard deal, vacating one of Toronto’s three two-way spots.

Smith signed a contract with the Raptors last month, but it was unclear if the former Zag would be in the mix to join the NBA team in Toronto or if he’d be suiting up for the G League Raptors 905.

With his two-way contract, Smith will likely split time between the Raptors and Raptors 905, with the ability to play in up to 50 games for the NBA team in Toronto.

“Thank you Jesus… you get all the GLORY,” Smith posted on X after the news was made public on Monday. “Toronto I need some food spots.”

After four stints in the G League with the Rip City Remix (Portland Trail Blazers), Wisconsin Herd (Milwaukee Bucks), Memphis Hustle (Memphis Grizzlies) and Long Island Nets (Brooklyn Nets), Smith signed a 10-day contract with Brooklyn on March 13 and eventually inked a standard, two-year deal when his 10-day expired.

The guard started in four of his 15 games for Brooklyn, averaging 8.3 points, 3.4 rebounds and 3.3 assists while shooting 48.5% from the field and 43.5% from the 3-point line. Smith hit double figures in six games and posted a 19-point, 10-rebound double-double on April 10 against the Milwaukee Bucks.

Smith had college stints at Wright State and Chattanooga before transferring to Gonzaga for his final season of eligibility in 2022-23. The guard played in 37 games, averaging 8.7 ppg, 3.6 rpg and 1.4 apg en route to earning West Coast Conference Sixth Man of the Year honors.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Graham Ike reportedly signs two-way contract with Golden State Warriors
Gonzaga.summary:
After a successful audition with the Golden State Warriors at NBA Summer League, Gonzaga’s Graham Ike will stick with the Western Conference franchise during his rookie season.

Ike has reportedly signed a two-year, two-way contract with the Warriors, according to Aryan of The Consensus NBA Substack newsletter.

The All-American forward is filling the third and final two-way spot on Golden State’s roster after the Warriors inked guard LJ Cryer and forward Malevy Leons to two-way deals.

Under the terms of his two-way contract, Ike will be able to play up to 50 games for Golden State’s NBA team in 2026-27, while also appearing for the G League Santa Cruz Warriors based roughly 75 miles away from the team’s home venue in San Francisco.

Ike may not have been a top candidate to earn a two-way deal with the Warriors after signing an undrafted Exhibit 10 contract with the organization in June, but he strengthened his chances over eight games – and eight starts – at the California Classic and Las Vegas Summer League.

The reigning West Coast Conference Player of the Year, Ike averaged 9.3 points, 7.2 rebounds and 1.8 assists at both Summer Leagues, helping guide Golden State to a championship run in Las Vegas. Ike tallied 10 points and 11 rebounds in a Vegas Summer League semifinal against former GU teammate Anton Watson and the Los Angeles Lakers before scoring six points with nine rebounds against former Washington State wing Cedric Coward and the Memphis Grizzlies.

“Graham does give you that kind of old school, on the block, he can score it around the paint,” Warriors Summer League coach Khalid Robinson said od Ike. “I think he’s also shown in Summer League his ability to get on the perimeter, make plays as far as it’s a dribble handoff, he’s making the right reads and then diving into the pocket.

“I think he gives you a little bit of both and I just love his overall energy and competitiveness and kind of the joy he plays with. He’s just a really good human being and a guy you enjoy having around.”

Golden State could be an ideal situation for Ike, who joins a veteran frontcourt that includes 31-year-old Kristaps Porzingis, 36-year-old Draymond Green and 40-year-old Al Horford. Those three combined to play just 128 of a possible 246 games last season due to injuries and load management.

The Warriors’ frontcourt will also include 11th overall draft pick Yaxel Lendeborg, who started alongside Ike at Summer League, and Brazilian forward Gui Santos, who played in 68 games for Golden State last season.

By the end of his fifth college season, Ike was the sport’s active career scoring and rebounding leader, totaling 2,575 points and 1,1144 rebounds over two years at Wyoming and three more at Gonzaga.

Ike led the Zags in scoring each of the last three seasons, averaging 16.5 ppg in 2023-24, 17.3 in 2024-25 and 19.9 in 2025-26. He doubled on up on postseason WCC awards, earning the league’s Player of the Year before being named the Most Outstanding Player at the conference tournament. Ike was also a finalist for the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Center of the Year Award and named a Third Team All-American by the Associated Press and NABC.

Gonzaga.title: Women’s Basketball Announces 2026-27 Non-Conference Schedule
Gonzaga women release nonconference schedule, including games at Stanford, Arizona State and Michigan State
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga released its women’s basketball nonconference schedule Monday for the 2026-27 season, and it shapes up as possibly the most challenging out-of-conference slate the Zags have had under coach Lisa Fortier.

Fortier begins her 13th season with a nonconference schedule that features six teams that finished in the top 100 of the NET last season with four teams earning NCAA Tournament berths.

Gonzaga’s three most attractive nonconference dates are road games – at Stanford (Nov. 15), at Arizona State (Dec. 6) and a men’s/women’s multi-event doubleheader vs. Michigan State (Dec. 19), the Acrisure Challenge, in Palm Desert, California.

Eight of 15 nonconference games are at McCarthey Athletic Center. Gonzaga was going to have a 16th nonconference game – the maximum allowed with 16 conference games – but a third opponent in the North Shore Classic in Hawaii – Gonzaga’s holiday tournament this year – pulled out last minute.

Whether Gonzaga lands a one-off additional nonconference game remains to be seen.

Gonzaga starts the season Oct. 27 with an exhibition game against Westmont College from Santa Barbara, California.

The Zags’ first three games are at home against North Dakota State (Nov. 2), a return game from last year’s season opener, Idaho (Nov. 6) and UC Riverside (Nov. 8), a return game from a year ago.

Gonzaga follows with two road games at Grand Canyon (Nov. 13) and Stanford.

After taking a year off from its traditional nonconference series with Montana, the Grizzlies visit Gonzaga on Nov. 18. The Zags have won 12 straight in the series.

Then the Zags are off for Hawaii where they will take on the host Rainbows (Nov. 21) and California (Nov. 23).

Gonzaga then makes the short trip to Cheney to face Eastern Washington (Nov. 29), concluding the November portion of the schedule. The Zags have won 20 straight against EWU.

An Ivy League school visits when Yale (Dec. 4) comes to town.

Two days later Gonzaga visits Arizona State to complete a two-year deal.

Gonzaga has just one former West Coast Conference opponent on its schedule, but it’s a good one when Loyola Marymount, which won the regular-season championship last year. LMU visits Dec. 10.

Following the neutral-court game against Michigan State, Gonzaga concludes nonconference play with two home games – against South Dakota State (Dec. 30), which is always a test, and St. Thomas (Jan. 2) from the Summit League.

Gonzaga was 5-4 last year against teams it was scheduled to play the first two months of the season.

Fortier is four wins shy of becoming the all-time winningest women’s basketball coach at Gonzaga (313-84), eclipsing Kelly Graves (316-136), whom Fortier succeeded.

Times and television information for the nonconference games will be released at a later date.

Pac-12 Conference play begins in early January.

Oregon State.title: Jesse Legree Continues To Set Records For Oregon State Football
Oregon State.summary:
En route to a 4-2 record for Oregon State football, true freshman wide receiver Jesse Legree has been one of the most electrifying players in the country.  The Baltimore native became the first Oregon State wide receiver ever to post over 100 receiving yards in six consecutive games, something not even legendary Beavers like Brandin Cooks and Mike Hass were able to do back in their day.

This week on State of the Beavs, we react to the incredible pace that Legree has set for himself while leading the nation in both receiving yards and touchdowns. We'll also react to Oregon State's thorough beatdown of San Diego State by a score of 66-14 this past weekend, which has made fans realize JaMarcus Shephard's talk of chasing a Pac-12 title is more than simply talk.

Ahead of the Oregon State-Washington State contest this week, we'll predict how things might go against Kirby Moore's squad, and look forward to the reunion with former Beavs head coach Trent Bray.

All that, plus the five games that you need to watch in college football this weekend. Go Beavs.

Braden Atkinson and Jesse Legree continued their impressive run of form and the tight ends also got heavily involved en route to the 56-26 result. Time to review that result and what else worked for JaMarcus Shephard to get his team to a 3-2 record on the year.

This Saturday, the Beavers host a 2-3 San Diego State squad, who are coming off of a dramatic 31-29 win over the Texas State Bobcats. In addition to our thoughts, you'll hear clips from Shephard's media availability, as well as offensive coordinator Mitch Dahlen and defensive coordinator Mike MacIntyre.

All that, plus a look at the five college football games that Matt Bagley thinks you should watch this weekend.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football is 0-2, But The Culture is Changing
Oregon State.summary:
Two weeks into the new college football season, JaMarcus Shephard's Oregon State Beavers are 0-2. Hanging tough with two ranked power conference teams is certainly better than being blown out, it has become clear in the days since the Texas Tech loss that moral victories are not what the program is chasing. 

This week on State of the Beavs, your host Matt Bagley reacts to the signs of progress that the Beavers showed in their home opener loss to Texas Tech. Also hear comments from Shephard himself and linebacker Dylan Layne, both of whom noted they intend to change the larger perception of the program.

It's also time to prepare for the non-conference finale against Montana at Reser Stadium this week, and look ahead to the Pac-12 schedule that begins next weekend. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Good, Bad, & Unknown After Oregon State's Loss At Houston
Oregon State.summary:
The Oregon State football program started the season this past weekend with a 33-20 loss against a nationally ranked Houston Cougars team.  The Beavers certainly had their share of missed opportunities, but it was an overall competent performance that wasn't out of reach until the final ten minutes. This week on State of the Beavs, your host Matt Bagley dives into the good things, the bad things, and the questions about this year's Oregon State football team yet to be answered. 

You'll also hear the audio from Beavs head coach JaMarcus Shephard's Monday media availability following the loss. Bagley also looks ahead to Week Two, when the Beavers have another incredibly tough Texas opponent as the Texas Tech Red Raiders make the trip to Corvallis. Go Beavs.

Washington State.title: Ahead of WSU and Boise State's first Pac-12 clash, a look back at the first seven matchups
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When Washington State takes the field this weekend against No. 21 Boise State, the Cougars will be in for a lot of firsts.

It’ll be WSU’s first time hosting Boise State since 2017, when the late Tyler Hilinski came off the bench to lead a wild comeback. It’ll be the first time that Cougar coach Kirby Moore has faced the Broncos, for whom he played in the early 2010s. It will also be quarterback Owen Eshelman’s first home start after taking over the reins last weekend.

But what about the previous matchups between the Cougs and Broncos, who will be meeting for the first time as Pac-12 foes? The teams have only clashed seven times before. WSU owns a 5-2 record in the matchup.

Here is a look back at all seven games, in chronological order.

1997: WSU wins a blowout in Pullman, 58-0

In former WSU quarterback Ryan Leaf’s senior season, the Cougars started 7-0 and wound up in the Rose Bowl. They laid the foundation for that magical season in late September, when they handed the Broncos a 58-0 loss, to this day BSU’s largest loss in program history and still the last time the program has been shut out in one game.

All told, Leaf completed 17 of 30 passes for 289 yards and three touchdowns, and the Cougars churned out 209 more yards and two touchdowns on the ground. Michael Black piled up 17 carries for 141 yards and two total touchdowns, while receiver Kevin McKenzie caught six passes for 101 yards and two touchdowns.

Also notable from that game: WSU kicker Rian Lindell connected on a 57-yard field goal. That put the Cougs up 17-0 in the second quarter.

The game also featured this interesting twist: Boise State kicker Todd Belcastro, a product of Mead High in Spokane, was not recruited by WSU and coach Mike Price. Ahead of the game, he gave this quote to the Idaho Statesman: “I hate the Cougars. I really do. I’m going to wear my Washington hat on the sideline Saturday after we win. I’m going to sign a football, put the score on it, and hand it to Price.”

1998: WSU follows up with a close win in Boise

In the following year, the Cougars traveled to the blue turf in Boise, where they emerged with a 33-21 win. The visitors were down 7-6 at halftime, but thanks to a 27-point second half, they won by a relatively comfortable margin.

In the fourth quarter, WSU went up by two scores on a touchdown pass from Steve Birnbaum to Leaford Hackett. Moments later, the Broncos drew within one score on a fumble recovery for a touchdown, only for the Cougars to put the game away with an explosive 79-yard touchdown rush from DeJuan Gillmore.

“They were blitzing us on just about every play in the first quarter,” said WSU coach Mike Price, whose team moved to 2-0 with that win. “That was keeping the quarterback off balance. He wasn’t able to get his feet set and make the plays we had to make.”

2000: Cougars eke out close win at Martin Stadium

In the final minute of a 35-35 game, WSU’s offense found itself at the Boise State 1-yard line.

“There was no doubt that we were going to go for it,” WSU coach Mike Price said.

The Cougars made their coach look wise, scoring on a short rush by Adam Hawkins, putting the hosts up by the final margin of 42-35. They could have kicked a field goal, but decided against it, giving their defense some extra wiggle room for the Broncos’ final drive.

In that one, WSU quarterback Jason Gesser completed 21 of 30 passes for 290 yards and two touchdowns, playing through concussion symptoms from the third quarter on.

2001: WSU spoils BSU coach Dan Hawkins’ debut with 41-20 victory

In this one, the visiting Cougars at one point ran off 28 points to secure what turned into a blowout 41-20 win, handing the Broncos a loss in new coach Dan Hawkins’ first home game at the helm of the program.

Some highlights from this game: Linebacker Raonall Smith returned an interception 54 yards for an interception, Jason Gesser found James Price for a 55-yard touchdown and, in the third quarter, Collin Henderson took a lateral from Gesser in the backfield, then threw it to Nakoa McElrath, who scored on a 71-yard play to give the Cougs a 41-13 lead.

2016: Cougars’ late rally not enough in 31-28 loss

WSU and Boise State didn’t meet again for another 15 years, but the game was worth the wait. In the third quarter, the Broncos went up 24-7, only for the Cougars to come roaring back, scoring three touchdowns to pull within three in the final moments.

But it wasn’t enough for WSU, which fell in a 31-28 defeat, quarterback Luke Falk’s final desperation heave going incomplete. For the game, Falk completed 55 of 71 passes for 480 yards, four touchdowns and one interception, which turned into a long pick-six by BSU cornerback Tyler Horton.

With under a minute to go in the fourth frame, BSU inexplicably kept throwing. The Cougars made former Shadle Park High star quarterback Brett Rypien pay, getting an interception from Charleston White in the end zone.

That gave the Cougs new life in the final minute, but with a few seconds to play, Falk had to launch one deep. It hit the blue turf, sealing the Broncos’ win.

“It’s like a boxer if he’s really good at hitting the bag, and then all of a sudden he fights a boxing match and he won’t throw any blows. That’s who we are,” the late WSU coach Mike Leach said. “We have to be a tougher football team and right now we’re not. Right now we’ve got a bunch of good, nice, jolly guys who will work their asses off, at times, but as soon as anybody hits them or there’s any adversity, we fold.”

2017: Hilinski comes off the bench to lead wild triple-overtime comeback

Where to start with WSU’s 47-44 triple-overtime win in 2017? The Cougars found themselves trailing 31-10 with a shade under 11 minutes to go, only to come back to tie it and send the game to overtime, doing so on a crazy series of scoring plays.

Early in the fourth frame, BSU lineman Curtis Weaver recovered a Luke Falk fumble and returned it for a touchdown. Falk was injured on the play and did not return to the game, paving the way for the late backup Tyler Hilinski to come off the bench and lead the rest of the comeback.

The Cougars drew within two scores on a 17-yard pass from Hilinski to Jamire Calvin. That’s about when things got weird. Later, Rypien stumbled and tried a shovel pass, which was promptly picked off by WSU linebacker Peyton Pelluer, who returned it for a touchdown. That trimmed the Broncos’ lead to 31-24.

Things got even crazier from there. With about three minutes left, WSU punted, but the ball caromed off a Boise State player and was recovered by the Cougs. A few plays later, Hilinski found running back Jamal Morrow for the game-tying touchdown.

Then, after the teams played to a draw after two overtimes, the Cougars forced the Broncos into a field goal in the third. They won on their possession, thanks to a 22-yard pass from Hilinski to Morrow, who jetted to the end zone and dove across the pylon for the winning score.

A few months later, Hilinski died by suicide, making this win extra special for his family and WSU.

2024: Ashton Jeanty boosts Heisman case in BSU’s 45-24 win over WSU

In the teams’ most recent clash, things were interesting in the fourth quarter, when quarterback John Mateer unleashed a deep touchdown pass to receiver Kyle Williams, helping the visiting Cougars claw within 24-17.

But thanks to Boise State’s runaway fourth frame, that’s as close as they got, good for a 45-24 BSU win.

In this one, Bronco running back Ashton Jeanty torched the Cougar defense for 259 yards rushing for four touchdowns, helping his case for the Heisman Trophy, finishing second in that race.

Washington State.title: How does WSU's defense match up with No. 21 Boise State's rushing attack? Look no further than tackling
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When Khamari Terrell makes a tackle in space, for a brief moment, he enters a world all by himself. Washington State’s veteran cornerback will usually lower his head, staring down into the turf, maybe closing his eyes, closing himself off to the chaos unfolding around him.

Then he usually takes his hands and slaps himself on the helmet. Once. Twice. Lets his energy seep off him like condensation off a glass of ice water.

Then he rejoins the action, ready to make another play for the Cougars, for whom he’s playing his fifth and final season of college football.

“I think it’s big, especially in college, just knowing that the corners have to tackle every game,” Terrell said earlier this week. “Especially this week, I’m gonna make it noticed that you’re not gonna be able to just run to my side and just think that you’re gonna get a big gain or anything.”

Terrell and the WSU defense will get a chance to prove it this weekend, when No. 21 Boise State comes to town for a showdown, the teams’ first clash in Pullman since 2017, the night the late Tyler Hilinski came off the bench to lead the Cougars to a triple-overtime comeback.

Here’s the short version of why Terrell and his fellow defensive backs, like cornerback Jalil Tucker and safety Jaylen Thomas, will have to come up big for their team: The Broncos own one of the country’s best rushing attacks, spearheaded by junior tailback Dylan Riley, who ranks second nationwide with 139 rushing yards per game. As a team, the Broncos’ 234 rushing yards per contest ranks ninth in the country.

That figures to put quite the strain on this WSU defense, which was gashed last weekend, giving up 48 points to Oregon State’s prolific offense in a three-score loss. But for the Cougars, as they prepare for their next outing, it’s not all about preventing scoring. It’s about one of Terrell’s favorite parts of the game: tackling.

All things considered, WSU (1-6, 0-3 Pac-12) has done a fine job of that this season. The Cougars have earned a Pro Football Focus tackling grade of 61.4, which ranks No. 93 nationwide, fifth in the Pac-12. They’ve turned in some gems of tackling outings, including in their loss to Fresno State earlier this season, when they missed just three total tackles.

In fact, some of the WSU defenders who have logged the most snaps are also the ones who have tackled the best. Veteran linebacker Keith Brown, who leads the team with 418 snaps, has missed only six tackles. Terrell, who has played 339 snaps, has whiffed only three times. And redshirt freshman nickelback Jamarey Smith, who has 313 snaps, has missed only one tackle all season.

So from a 30,000-foot view, the Cougars have done well to tackle, and their coaches deserve credit for that: defensive coordinator Trent Bray, cornerbacks coach Brandyn Thompson and defensive line coach Eti Ena, among others. Past Cougar teams have not tackled particularly well – Jake Dickert’s 2024 team finished the season ranked fifth-to-last in PFF’s tackling grades, while Jimmy Rogers’ 2025 club finished dead last – so for the program, this represents a key step in the right direction.

“Game to game, you gotta be prepared to tackle,” Terrell said, “especially going against a team that runs a lot. So just be physical and just shut down the side of the field and just stop the run, so they won’t try to keep running to that side.”

The only problem at hand: Boise State’s playmakers have excelled at forcing missed tackles. In six games, Riley has forced 28 whiffs, which ranks second in the Pac-12. Riley has forced 18. They have excelled in space, and while the Cougars have usually done well to tackle in those types of settings, they aren’t coming off a particularly encouraging outing on that front.

In WSU’s loss to Oregon State last weekend, the Cougs missed 18 tackles, one off their most of the season, which came in a season-opening loss to Washington back in early September. In Corvallis, safety Jeremiah Bernard led the way with five whiffs, while fellow safety Jaylen Thomas followed with three and two players missed two tackles apiece: linebacker Isaiah Hung and cornerback Kai Rapolla.

How will those two realities clash on Saturday afternoon on the Palouse? If the Cougars can’t make tackles in space, they might be in for a long day, and as 14-point underdogs, they’re expected to meet that fate anyway. But it’s an interesting conversation because of one key development: Bray’s unit has done a stellar job of stacking up runs up the middle.

That’s where some of the Cougars’ best defenders play, from defensive tackles like Jirah Leaupepetele and Kaden Beatty to defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk, which is why opponents haven’t enjoyed much success running up the middle this season. Even Brown, a linebacker, has graded out as the Cougars’ best run defender, with a mark of 79.9.

It’s on the outsides where the Cougs have had less luck, at least in their most recent showing. To turn that fortune around – to reverse the fortune of this entire season – WSU defenders will have to clean that up. Maybe that’s where Terrell, a veteran cornerback, could come in handy.

Washington State.title: How did WSU QB Owen Eshelman engineer such a strong showing in his first start? Three things stood out most
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – In the aftermath of quarterback Owen Eshelman’s first start, an electric showing in his Washington State group’s fourth straight loss over the weekend, the reactions came showering in like a typhoon.

He’s actually airing it out!

He looks poised in the pocket!

Look how sharp the Cougs’ offense looks!

Indeed, Eshelman guided WSU to 30 offensive points, the team’s most all season. That wasn’t enough to prevent the Cougs from falling short again, this time to the tune of a 48-30 final margin, but Eshelman looked accurate. He was willing to look for the deep ball. He executed a couple really well.

For the Cougars, that represented a firm step in the right direction, an indication that head coach Kirby Moore made the right call pivoting away from Caden Pinnick and swapping in Eshelman. Should coaches have made that move sooner in the season? Probably, and that conversation has been fleshed out in all kinds of ways.

“We’re not looking in the rearview mirror,” Moore said after Saturday’s game on that topic. “We gotta keep building on where we’re at right now.”

What isn’t as immediately obvious at first blush is how different the Cougs’ passing attack was with Eshelman at the controls. He aired it out, sure, but how much of a change did that represent for WSU? How did his accuracy bolster the offense? And how did he navigate the pocket?

As Washington State prepares for its homecoming game, a home showdown with first-place Boise State this weekend, those questions are worth exploring. Do the Cougs have a shot at pulling the upset? They might be 12.5-point underdogs, but Eshelman and the life he brings to his offense could be reason to believe the answer might be yes.

1. Eshelman looked to push the ball downfield

Perhaps the most striking part of Eshelman’s performance, the development that might have made you say “wow” right away, came in his readiness to stretch the field vertically. Pinnick wasn’t just shaky at this in his six starts; he wasn’t even willing to do it.

Think about this: In WSU’s loss to Utah State earlier this month, Pinnick attempted only six passes 10 yards or further downfield, according to PFF. That included zero passes 20 yards or deeper. It was clear that he wasn’t comfortable in the pocket. He didn’t trust his eyes, didn’t trust his arm.

Think about it this way: In the country, 61 QBs have dropped back at least 200 times. Among that group, Pinnick is the only one to attempt fewer than 20 passes of at least 20 yards downfield. His official numbers on those types of throws: 2-for-16 for 78 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions.

On Saturday, Eshelman tried 16 passes at least 10 yards downfield, connecting on six of them. That isn’t a great completion rate – just 38% – but his willingness to try those opened up a lot for the Cougars’ offense. On one play in the first half, Eshelman lofted one downfield for receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who hauled it in for a 40-yard touchdown pass.

“It was a great look,” Eshelman said after the game about the touchdown pass. “Had a couple different options there, and he ended up popping and was really excited for him on that touchdown, and just the offense was clicking well.”

Outside of Pinnick’s one FBS touchdown toss, a 46-yard completion to Ganashamoorthy on which an Arizona defender fell down in coverage, that was the Cougars’ longest passing scoring play all season. Eshelman showed great touch on that pass, as well as a layered 24-yard throw, also to Ganashamoorthy. It was obvious he felt confident letting throws like that fly.

On another play in Saturday’s game, a first-and-10 near the redzone, Eshelman showed the same willingness. He dropped back and spotted an open receiver in Daniel Blood, so Eshelman reared back and put the same kind of nice touch on this pass, finding Blood for a 23-yard gain. Four plays later, QB Julian Dugger came in for a short touchdown plunge.

2. Eshelman’s pocket presence stood out in a big way

One of the central problems facing Pinnick, especially in his last handful of starts, was his pocket presence. He often ran himself into sacks. He held onto the ball too long. He didn’t throw it away when he had the opportunity, leading to even more sacks. Sometimes he was too indecisive to avoid a rusher headed right for him.

Even with one fewer game under his belt, Pinnick is still tied for the nationwide lead in QB-fault sacks with 11, according to PFF.

Contrast that with the one game of Eshelman, who took just one sack of that variety, according to PFF. He was sacked on two other occasions, which were the fault of the Cougars’ offensive line, which played without injured left tackle Ashton Tripp.

In fact, some of Eshelman’s best plays came on the ground, when he identified pressure and bailed at the right times. He recorded three rushes of 20-plus yards: a 22-yard scramble, a 41-yard burst and a 19-yard read option, which he took 20 yards into the end zone for his first career rushing touchdown at the college level.

“Obviously there’s a lot of situational stuff with that, and knowing when it’s OK to punt, knowing when you might need to take a shot,” Eshelman said. “There were definitely some missed opportunities tonight, some times that I thought I did a good job, and we’ll keep working on that and growing in it.”

3. He didn’t let a slow start bog him down

How many times did we see this kind of situation unfold with Pinnick at the controls? He’d slog through something of a slow start, which is normal for any quarterback, and that kind of uneven beginning would follow him around the rest of the game.

At least from an outsider’s perspective, it seemed easy for Pinnick to let slow starts color the rest of his outing, never letting him find a rhythm later in the game.

Eshelman was hardly perfect in Saturday’s game. He missed on each of his first three passes, costing his team early chances, which was one of the ways Oregon State mounted an early 17-0 lead. He targeted Ganashamoorthy on each of his first three throws, all of which sailed wide of the mark, including a third-down throw that led to a punt.

But Eshelman didn’t let that throw him off for the rest of the game. He went on to complete 8 of his next 10 passes, including the aforementioned 24-yarder to Ganashamoorthy and a 14-yard toss to tight end Jack Pedersen.

Also in that stretch, he showed nice patience in the pocket, taking the shorter throws when they were there. That was another part of Eshleman’s game that stood out, to which he even alluded after the game: He seemed to understand when it’s OK to throw checkdowns and shorter passes.

That kept the Cougars’ offense moving.

Washington State.title: Two rookie coaches, two wildly different starts | Pac-12 football midseason awards
Washington State.summary:
The midpoint of the inaugural football season for the new Pac-12 does not exist, at least not in a clean, easily identifiable fashion.

Half the teams have played seven games; half have played six.

Half have played three conference matchups; half have played two.

But against the full sweep of a competition calendar that runs from Labor Day weekend (for everyone) through Thanksgiving weekend (for all but two teams), the end of Week 7 marks a reasonable middle.

With that, the Hotline presents our Pac-12 midseason report, in which we highlight the best and worst, key themes and standout performers.

Top storyline: CFP relevance. Two teams, Boise State and Oregon State, remain in pursuit of a berth in the College Football Playoff. The Broncos (5-1) have a quality loss at Oregon and key wins over Memphis and Western Michigan. If they win out, a bid should follow. The Beavers (5-2) have a trickier path but will be in play if they finish with two losses. The conference could not have realistically asked for more at this point.

Best coach: Oregon State’s JaMarcus Shephard. The rookie coach has made a series of master-class moves with his staff and roster and could land on the short list for national Coach of the Year if the Beavers keep winning. Also considered: Boise State’s Spencer Danielson

Hottest seat: Washington State’s Kirby Moore. The rookie coach has made a series of deeply flawed decisions with his staff and roster. We don’t expect Moore to get fired after the season, although if the current trajectory continues, you could make the case for dismissal. Also considered: San Diego State’s Sean Lewis

Best offensive player: Oregon State WR Jesse Legree. The freshman has been a revelation and is generating second-tier Heisman Trophy support. He leads the country in receiving yards and touchdowns – not bad for a three-star prospect. Also considered: Oregon State QB Braden Atkinson, Boise State TB Dylan Riley and Texas State TB Torrance Burgess

Best defensive player: San Diego State LB Sione Hala. The senior leads the Pac-12 and is fifth in the country in tackles (68) and recorded sacks against both James Madison and Oregon State. He also forced a fumble against Fresno State that led to an Aztecs field goal in what became a three-point win. Also considered: Oregon State edge Takari Hickle and Fresno State lineman Dylan Hampsten.

Top transfer: Oregon State QB Braden Atkinson. The Mercer transfer threw 34 touchdown passes last year for an FCS team that won nine games, so he’s not exactly a rookie. But Atkinson’s field vision and downfield accuracy mesh perfectly with Legree’s skills. Also considered: Nobody

Best game: San Diego State 31, Texas State 29. The Oct. 3 affair in Snapdragon Stadium featured a series of momentum shifts, 40 points in the second half, just two turnovers and a stellar individual effort from Texas State quarterback Brad Jackson. Also considered: Boise State 38, Fresno State 31

Best win: Boise State 38, Memphis 20. If the Pac-12’s best team is drawn into a resume showdown with the American’s best team for a playoff berth, the Broncos’ Week 2 head-to-head win over a top American team could loom large. Also considered: Boise State over Western Michigan and Texas State over North Texas

Worst loss: Idaho State 29, Utah State 17. Double-digit home losses to FCS opponents are always ugly. Add 11 penalties and four turnovers, and this was an all-systems failure for the Aggies. Also considered: None. (We didn’t have the stomach to continue the research.)

Best performance: Oregon State WR Jesse Legree. The freshman’s breakout game came in Week 2, when he sliced and diced Texas Tech’s secondary for 240 yards receiving and two touchdowns. Also considered: Boise State TB Dylan Riley (Memphis), Texas State TB Torrance Burgess (North Texas) and San Diego State TB Javion Kinnard (James Madison)

Worst luck: San Diego State. Misfortune during the football season typically takes the form of injuries, officiating blunders or players short-circuiting in some fashion. When was the last time a team was derailed by the mumps? Probably the 1950s. Goodness, gracious.
