Washington State.title: WSU WR Darrius Clemons, OT Ashton Tripp questionable with injuries, plus other notes
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State’s offense is looking better, but that group may not be at full strength this weekend when No. 21 Boise State comes to town.

Left tackle Ashton Tripp is day-to-day with an ankle injury, WSU coach Kirby Moore said Monday, while wide receiver Darrius Clemons is dealing with his own ankle injury. Medical staff is “determining the extent of that injury here early this week,” Moore said.

Tripp missed WSU’s road loss to Oregon State on Saturday, which prompted Washington transfer Maximus McCree to take his place, marking the first time someone other than Tripp has played left tackle for WSU since 2023. Tripp is a key cog on the Cougars’ offensive line.

Clemons’ injury could also be costly for the Cougs, who were already running low on depth at the wide receiver spot thanks to a season-ending ACL tear to Tony Freeman in the Sept. 6 Apple Cup. Clemons played just 12 snaps in Saturday’s game before coming out with his injury, getting carted to the locker room and returning to the bench with crutches by his side.

Listed at 6-foot-3 and 217 pounds, Clemons had played a big role in the pass-catching department, hauling in 20 receptions for 218 yards, starting in all seven games. If Clemons can’t play this weekend against Boise State, the Cougars will ask more from receivers Daniel Blood, Tank Hawkins and Branden Ganashamoorthy, the latter of whom posted 11 catches for 147 yards last weekend – both career highs.

A couple other receivers could get more reps, Moore added , West Georgia transfer Jordan Dees and walk-on Caleb Northcroft. A year after reeling in 35 receptions for 508 yards and three touchdowns at the FCS level, Dees has played just four snaps this season, all of which came against FCS Duquesne in Week 3.

Asked what’s preventing Dees from seeing a bigger role, Moore said , “There’s guys ahead of him right now on the depth chart. He’s gotta work to continue to be consistent, just like his teammates, and that’s the big focus for him is just focusing on doing his job, alignment, assignment, obviously playing catch with the quarterbacks and being on the same page.”

• In other injury news, defensive ends Malachi Wrice and Michael Hughes are expected to play “full speed” this weekend, Moore said. After missing five straight games, Hughes returned against Oregon State, posting one pressure in 30 snaps. Wrice, who has been out since Week 2, suited up but didn’t play.

That’s a meaningful development for WSU, which needs some depth behind starting pass rushers Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk, who combined for five pressures against Oregon State.

• On Monday, Moore also said name, image and likeness earnings have no bearing on playing time: “No, the best players are gonna play. We’ve had those evaluations at a number of positions, whether that’s quarterback, receiver, D-tackle. It’s really about who gives us the best opportunity to win.”

That has been something of a discussion lately in the wake of the coaches’ decision to bench QB Caden Pinnick, a transfer from UC Davis, in favor of redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman. Did NIL play a factor in Pinnick remaining the starter for six games? Moore said no.

So what separated those two in fall camp, and how much of what Eshelman put on display in Saturday’s game – completing 32 of 49 passes for 289 yards, two touchdowns and one garbage-time interception, plus 15 carries for 136 yards and one score – did he seem capable of earlier in the year?

“He definitely showed flashes,” Moore said. “I think the one thing, and he would say it as well, in fall camp there, there was probably some (issues) in terms of taking care of the football. Probably had a few more than we wanted, and he’s definitely grown from that. Obviously, it starts in practice and preparing like you’re the starter, and he continued to do that throughout the season.”

In fall camp, Eshelman did commit an interception or two, including coming inches away from another at the hands of safety Jaylen Thomas. But Pinnick also had his share of turnover problems, including a three-interception (two tipped) outing in the team’s second and final scrimmage.

Washington State.title: WSU set to host Boise State for first time since 2017 | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s home game against No. 21 Boise State on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

Still looking for its first FBS win of the season, WSU (1-6, 0-3) returns home for the first time in three weeks to host No. 21 Boise State (5-1, 2-0), which was idle last week. It’s the Cougars’ and Broncos’ first time meeting in Pullman since 2017, when the late Tyler Hilinski came off the bench to lead WSU to a triple-overtime win.

It’s a full-circle moment for WSU coach Kirby Moore, who played for the Broncos from 2009-13, which is also when he met quarterbacks coach Matt Miller and formed many of the connections that he uses today.

Where is it? Gesa Field in Pullman.

When is it? Kickoff is set for 3 p.m.

Where can I watch it? USA Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored? WSU opened as a 14-point underdog.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

In a 48-30 loss to Oregon State, WSU redshirt freshman quarterback Owen Eshelman got his first start, completing 32 of 49 passes for 289 yards, two touchdowns and one late interception in garbage time. He also racked up 136 rushing yards on 15 carries, sparking the Cougs’ offense to its most points against an FBS opponent all season.

The Cougars’ offense looked much improved, at least in the passing game, but it wasn’t enough to upset the Beavers and their prolific offense. OSU QB Braden Atkinson piled up 347 passing yards and three touchdowns, including a 90-yard strike to freshman Jesse Legree and an 88-yard completion to receiver AJ Newberry, both of which came after the Cougars elected to punt on fourth-and-short near midfield – making Moore pay for his conservative approach.

After those plays, WSU couldn’t climb out of an early hole, trailing 17-0 before the visitors got on the scoreboard with a short field goal from kicker Jack Stevens. The Cougars pulled to within three scores on a 40-yard touchdown pass from Eshelman to receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who finished with career highs in both receptions and receiving yards, but it was too little too late for Washington State.

“I would just say we lost there,” WSU cornerback Khamari Terrell said. “It wasn’t really we got beaten there. Just a little technical, little details. The look that we got and that they scored on, we’ve got multiple times in practice, just doing the little details. And the technique part, just staying on top and just executing there.”

Eshelman may have looked sharp on the ground, but it was another slow day for the WSU running back trio of Maxwell Woods, Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi, who combined for just 26 rushing yards on 13 carries. Against FBS opponents this year, they are averaging only 52 yards per game, a far cry from the elite trio they were projected to be headed into the season.

“The tailbacks need to be able to run the ball better, but that starts up front,” Moore said on Monday. “We gotta block better, and we gotta have our hands inside. We gotta win our one-on-one matchups. We gotta put the ball in the corner in the safeties, and then from a running back standpoint, we gotta make people miss as well. So it’s a combination of things there, but we gotta do a much better job.”

Scouting Boise State…

Under head coach Spencer Danielson and veteran quarterback Maddux Madsen, the Broncos have followed a season-opening loss to Oregon with five straight wins, most recently a 38-31 win over Fresno State on Oct. 10. That has landed Boise State squarely in the discussion for the College Football Playoff.

The strength of the Broncos’ team is their rushing attack, which is averaging 235 yards per game, ninth nationally and second in the Pac-12. Running back Dylan Riley ranks second in the country with 139 yards per game, totaling six touchdowns on the ground, and fellow tailback Sire Gaines has provided an additional three scores and 354 yards. Those two have spearheaded the Broncos’ offense all season.

In his third season as BSU’s full-time starting QB, Madsen has taken phenomenal care of the ball, throwing zero interceptions and 13 touchdowns. He’s completed 110 of 166 passes (66%) for 1,296 yards. He’s also only taken five sacks, an impressive feat from the Broncos’ offensive line, which has only been responsible for three sacks according to Pro Football Focus.

The Broncos’ ground game has become so dangerous in part because their running backs are hard to bring down. Riley has forced 28 missed tackles, according to PFF, which is second in the Pac-12. Gaines isn’t far behind, with 18. Combined with Madsen’s ability to avoid turnovers – BSU has lost only three turnovers, tied for second-fewest nationally – and you get a machine of an offense.

“They’ve got a really good front,” Moore said. “They have a good scheme. They’ve got good backs. They put the ball in the corner, and a lot of times the back makes the corner miss, whether it’s a move or he breaks a tackle, and both those guys, Sire Gaines as well. They both do a really good job with the ball in their hand.”

What happened last time?

In a 2024 matchup in Boise, former Bronco running back Ashton Jeanty ran ragged over the Cougars, piling up 259 yards and four touchdowns, boosting his Heisman Trophy case. The Cougars were within one score early in the fourth quarter, but the Broncos ran away with three straight touchdowns.

Washington State.summary:
Mountain West Freshman of the Year and sophomore guard Jake Hall scored 22 points on 8 of 10 shooting and the University of New Mexico Lobos Men’s basketball team beat the Washington State Cougars 92-64 in an exhibition game at The Pit in Albuquerque, New Mexico on Sunday. 

The Cougars never really stood a chance after the Lobos went on an 8-2 run to start the game, and pulled away with a 16-0 run with just under 14 minutes left in the first half.

Midway through the second half, the Cougs trailed by 42 points 80-38, their largest deficit of the game. 

Uriah Tennette hit a 3-pointer on the Lobos’ first possession but East Texas A&M senior transfer guard Ronnie Harrison replied with a layup to make it 3-2. 

But the Lobos separated themselves with a 16-point surge in a four-minute span in the first period started by redshirt freshman Imran Suljanovic’s 3-pointer at 13 minutes, 47 seconds. 

The Cougars stopped the bleeding when Dembele stole the ball from Hall, and connected with Houston on a fastbreak to make it 30-16. But WSU couldn’t recover and found themselves in a 25-point deficit entering halftime. 

Houston led WSU with 14 points and two assists, and Harrison added 12 points, four rebounds, and four assists for the Cougs. 

Andrew Cook leads Eagles to close win over CSU Bakersfield 

After missing all of last season with an ankle injury, and uncertainty surrounding his college eligibility this year, Andrew Cook shined in his 2026 season debut with the Eastern Washington Eagles, leading all players with 24 points in a 71-65 exhibition victory against CSU Bakersfield Roadrunners at Reese Court in Cheney on Sunday. 

Cook also added five rebounds to go with three assists. He was also a defensive force with a block early in the first half and two steals, including a critical one late in the second half that helped the Eagles retake the lead with just over three minutes remaining. 

Down 58-56 with 4 minutes, 7 seconds remaining, Cook stole the ball and was fouled by Tom Koppens on the fastbreak. Cook made his first free throw, but missed the second. But returning redshirt junior forward Emmett Marquardt got the offensive rebound, and Cook converted the layup to make it 59-58. EWU never trailed again. 

After a close first five minutes, the Eagles scored six straight thanks to a 3-pointer from Isak Homelius and found themselves up by eight 15-7 midway through the first half – their largest lead of the game. 

But the Roadrunners marched back, regaining the lead with 5 minutes, 25 seconds left in the first period after Malachi Richardson missed his 3-pointer, and Jaden Alexander converted his shot to make it 23-21. 

EWU and CSU Bakersfield exchanged leads, and the Eagles entered halftime down three.

Washington State.title: QB Owen Eshelman, WR Branden Ganashamoorthy spark Cougs' offense in loss to Oregon State
Washington State.summary:
CORVALLIS, Ore. – Branden Ganashamoorthy insisted the sunlight was no problem. When he strode open toward the Oregon State end zone, he said, all he saw was the ball. He tracked it in the air, on its descent, into his hands as he fell onto the black turf for six.

“When you’re in those moments,” Ganashamoorthy said, “it’s almost like tunnel vision. Everything kinda slows down. The amount of tennis balls, the amount of footballs I’ve caught. I feel like I can catch those balls almost blind.”

In his Washington State group’s 48-30 loss to Oregon State, the Cougars’ fourth straight loss, Ganashamoorthy enjoyed the best outing of his career: He logged 11 catches for 147 yards and the one score, which came on a 40-yard pass in the second quarter, pulling the Cougs to within 27-10.

It amounted to a huge day for Ganashamoorthy, an indicator of what he’s capable of. It also went a long way in illustrating how he accomplished it, finding a sharp rapport with quarterback Owen Eshelman, who made his first start. By his number, you would never have known it: He completed 32 of 49 passes for 289 yards, two touchdowns and one meaningless interception in garbage time. He also totaled 11 carries for 147 yards and another touchdown, racking up the second-most yards in one game by a WSU QB in program history.

A redshirt freshman from Oklahoma, Eshelman shattered expectations for his first real game action. He looked willing to air it out deep, which the Cougars didn’t get from Caden Pinnick, who started each of the first six games of the season. He made the right reads in the pocket, bailing at the right times to scramble for yards on the ground. And he made a fantastic decision on his rushing touchdown, pulling the ball and jetting straight into the end zone, cruising in for a 20-yard score.

“We just had a much better rhythm,” WSU coach Kirby Moore said of Eshelman’s outing and what it provided to the team. “That takes all 11 being on the same page, whether it’s communication, whether it’s in the run game, the RPOs, obviously the pass game. It’s about landmarks and alignments there with the receivers and guys winning versus man and the quarterback trusting them. Today it was much better on first and second down. Third down, obviously did a better job in the second half than the first half.”

“It was definitely excitement,” Eshelman said of his emotions headed into his first start. “Obviously Oregon State’s been playing really good football, and to have the opportunity to come here and showcase what our offense is capable of … There’s that Cougar mentality that we’re just gonna keep swinging, and I thought that showed up tonight, even with some missed opportunities. I was just really proud of all of our guys. We kept swinging, kept swinging, kept swinging, and making the most out of opportunities.”

In this one, Eshelman and the Cougars’ offense was hardly perfect. They converted just 7 of 17 third downs, and through three quarters, the number was 0-for-9. They still are getting almost nothing from the running back trio of Maxwell Woods, Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi, who combined for only 26 yards on 13 carries. Under a coach like Moore, who unlocked Missouri’s rushing game to incredible results in his three years as the Tigers’ offensive coordinator, that will raise eyebrows for all the wrong reasons.

The Cougars also slogged through four three-and-outs, but their biggest problems didn’t center on things they did. They were about things they didn’t. On two spots in the first half, fourth-and-1 from the Beaver 48 and fourth-and-3 from the Cougar 49, Moore chose to punt. In both scenarios, Oregon State turned those into long touchdowns, both on the very next play. Chalk those up to misses for Moore and his game management.

“No, I’ve got a ton of confidence in our defense,” Moore said about whether he regretted punting on those plays. “Obviously, when you punt the ball and they have the ball inside their 15-yard line, you get a stop, you’ve got great field position. That didn’t happen. Give them credit. They’ve got good players. They executed and made plays.”

But overall, WSU’s offense looked far more capable than it ever has this season. The Cougars’ 30 points are their most against FBS competition all season. Outside of Eshelman’s late interception, a truly meaningless development, they avoided turnovers for the first time all season. It’s clear that Eshelman is the right quarterback for this team.

With Eshelman at the controls, and with Ganashamoorthy playing one of his favorite targets, a few more wins could be on the docket for this group.

“With the new change at quarterback, obviously, I would say just meshing together,” Ganashamoorthy said. “Now that we have that set, Owen at quarterback, I’d say meetings and everything can start to flow a little bit easier. Practices and everything, with his leadership, I think everything will come together when it does.”

Washington State.title: WSU may have lost to Oregon State, but in QB Owen Eshelman’s first start, the Cougars grew up | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
CORVALLIS, Ore. – After each of his Washington State team’s first five games of the season, Kirby Moore strode up to the postgame microphone and sounded neutral. He sounded the same after his group’s loss to Utah State and after its win over FCS Duquesne. He talked like a coach whose team had just played to a tie.

After WSU’s 48-30 loss to Oregon State here on Saturday night, the Cougars’ fourth straight loss, he talked like a coach who was furious. He was far more animated, much more visibly frustrated with the way things had unfolded. He had never shown so much emotion, low as the bar is for the usually vanilla Moore.

Here’s a sampling.

What did you think of Owen Eshelman’s play in his first start?

“We had a much better rhythm,” Moore said. “I thought the first couple drives we had some chances there didn’t execute, and then finding completions, obviously extending plays. Thought there was some tempo elements to the offense, and we gotta keep building on that.”

Do you wish you would have pivoted to him sooner in the season?

“We’re not looking in the rearview mirror,” Moore said. “We gotta keep building on where we’re at right now.”

Regardless of what you think of those answers , understand this: Moore had never looked so fired up after a game. He looked comfortable expressing both his likes and dislikes, looked confident in explaining his decisions, questionable as some were. He looked more like a head coach.

Pair that with his decision to bench Pinnick and roll with Eshelman and you wind up with this conclusion from Saturday’s game: WSU grew up. The Cougars entered their next chapter with this game. They started the right quarterback. Their coach is beginning to look and sound more like a guy who believes in his system.

It’s a significant development for WSU, even if it’s true that these things took too long to happen. Did coaches wait too long to start Eshelman? Probably. Did Moore take too long to sound so convicted? Also likely. But Moore is a first-time head coach, and these are lessons he had to learn at some point. Give him credit for being open enough to apply them midseason.

Moore almost certainly knows that he stuck with Pinnick for too long, same as he knows that it was a mistake to punt it away on two fourth-and-short situations around midfield, both of which immediately led to long Oregon State touchdowns. He didn’t acknowledge either after the game – it’s not fair to expect him to, given the way that would affect cohesion in the locker room – but you can see him learning the right lessons. That matters for the Cougs, even in what is turning into a lost season, now at 1-6 overall and 0-3 in Pac-12 play.

Here is his response to whether he regretted punting it on fourth-and-1 from the OSU 48, then punting again on fourth-and-3, both of which turned into OSU touchdowns on the very next play: “No, I’ve got a ton of confidence in our defense. Obviously, when you punt the ball and they have the ball inside their 15-yard line, you get a stop, you’ve got great field position. That didn’t happen. Give them credit. They’ve got good players. They executed and made plays.”

Two things can be true. One: Moore understands he should not have punted in those spots, and if a similar situation arises next weekend against Boise State, expect him to go for it. Two: He expressed confidence in his defense, which is key to keeping this season from going completely off the rails. Sometimes you just have to back your guys, even if it sounds silly to the rest of the world.

Now let’s get to Eshelman, who looked electric in his first career start, completing 32 of 49 passes for 289 yards, two touchdowns and one meaningless interception in the final seconds with the game out of reach. He also carried 15 times for 136 yards and one more score, earning the second-most rushing yards by a WSU QB in program history. If you didn’t know this was Eshelman’s first start, and your friend told you mid-game, you’d call them a liar.

As he made play after play, as he connected with Branden Ganashamoorthy for a 40-yard touchdown pass and as he glided 20 yards into the end zone in the second half, you might have had this thought: Why didn’t they go with Eshelman sooner? Why did they stick with Pinnick so long?

All of those thoughts are normal to feel, and heck, there’s probably some level of truth in them. Eshelman looked tremendous in this game. He aired it out for a long touchdown. He made a great read to score with his legs. He oozes talent and potential. The Cougars probably have one or two more wins with Eshelman at the controls.

Still, keep this in mind: Eshelman was not clearly WSU’s best quarterback coming out of fall camp. At that time, he looked less like a guy who could have pulled this off and more like a second-year freshman still learning the ropes of playing QB at the FBS level. Which was totally fine. Tons of quarterbacks aren’t ready to play at this stage of their careers.

During fall camp, Pinnick was pretty obviously the team’s best quarterback. He had some turnover problems, but because Eshelman didn’t look ready and because Julian Dugger didn’t pose enough threat with his arm, Pinnick felt like the right choice. That’s why it was no surprise when he was announced as such.

You can also squint and see the logic in rolling with him as long as Moore did. Pinnick looked static and turnover-prone in all six games he played, but as the struggles became clear and Moore took over playcalling duties ahead of the Utah State game, maybe coaches wanted to see how he looked with Moore calling plays. If he didn’t look any better, the thinking might have gone, pivot away from him then. That’s what coaches did.

Now, about that logic. Against FBS competition, Pinnick never really looked sharp. After he lost two turnovers in a 26-6 loss to Fresno State, it was probably time to bench him. At that point, it was clear that the opponent wasn’t the one causing Pinnick to play so poorly. It was his decision-making, his inability to stretch the field, his lack of willingness to even look at passes downfield, and all of that had a downstream effect on the Cougs’ offense. It hearkened back to the Paul Wulff days, which is not a conversation Moore wants to be in.

Besides, Moore isn’t paid to learn lessons. He’s paid to win games. He made a mistake riding with Pinnick for so long. Based on the results, Moore probably made a mistake pursuing Pinnick in the first place.

But these are things Moore was always going to have to take time to learn. As a first-time head coach, he was going to need to learn how to identify the right quarterback. He was going to need to learn when to pivot away from that guy. He was going to need to learn that, when you’re 1-5 and 18.5-point underdogs, you don’t punt it from midfield and take opportunities away from your new – and very capable – quarterback.

In hiring a first-time head coach, WSU brass implicitly acknowledged all of that, too.

With Eshelman at the controls, the complexion of the rest of this season changes a bit for the Cougars. They don’t look like a team that can beat Boise State next weekend, but they do look like one that can beat San Diego State, Colorado State, even Texas State on the road. Maybe they would be gunning for bowl eligibility in those games if they had gone to Eshelman sooner. But Eshelman is here now, and that’s the right call from Moore.

Washington State.title: Oregon State quarterback Braden Atkinson's stellar season continues | Difference makers
Washington State.summary:
OSU QB Braden Atkinson

The sophomore transfer continued his remarkable debut season at the FBS level, completing 23 of 38 passes for 347 yards with three touchdowns and no turnovers. Atkinson, who won the Jerry Rice Award (FCS freshman of the year) at Mercer last season, entered the game leading the FBS in passing yards and TD throws, and he boosted his numbers on the season to 2,604 yards and 24 TDs with only two interceptions. Atkinson connected on seven completions of 15 yards or more, including a 90-yard scoring bomb in the first half to star freshman receiver Jesse Legree. Atkinson completed eight straight passes during one stretch in the second half, two for TDs, as the Beavers put the game away.

OSU RB AJ Newberry

A senior Vanderbilt transfer, Newberry had the most productive game of his collegiate career, producing 225 yards from scrimmage and a touchdown. The 6-foot-1, 200-pound Texas native was a problem for Cougar tacklers, averaging 9.5 yards on 11 carries for 105 yards on the ground, with long rushes of 30, 26 and 19 yards. He was also a threat in the passing game, recording five receptions for 120 yards. On a screen pass late in the second quarter, Newberry outraced everyone and hurdled the last WSU tackler on his way to an 88-yard touchdown, which extended Oregon State’s lead to 27-3, an insurmountable deficit for a Cougars team that found some offensive success with a new quarterback, but is still searching for consistency.

Washington State.title: Quarterback Owen Eshelman has encouraging debut, but Washington State defense struggles in loss at Oregon State | Instant reactions
Washington State.summary:
Washington State’s new quarterback showed some encouraging signs, but the Cougars couldn’t keep pace with Oregon State’s explosive offense. The Beavers built a big lead in the second quarter and rolled to a 48-30 Pac-12 Conference win on Saturday at Reser Stadium in Corvallis, Oregon, keeping WSU winless against FBS opponents.

Owen Eshelman distinguished himself as WSU’s best option at QB. The Cougars defense, facing one of the nation’s most productive outfits, had their worst game yet.

The Cougars (1-6, 0-3 Pac-12) get no reprieve next week when No. 23 Boise State comes to Pullman.

Cougs can’t contain Beavs potent offense

WSU surrendered season highs in points and yards (555). Defensive coordinator Trent Bray, the former coach at Oregon State, didn’t have answers in the first half against the Beavers offense, which scored on five of its first six possessions and went ahead 27-3 late in the second quarter.

Beavs breakout star QB Braden Atkinson was exceptional, as expected. He avoided mistakes and tested WSU’s deep coverage consistently, hitting on a tone-setting, 90-yard TD strike to star true freshman Jesse Legree, who finished with 108 yards and two TDs.

It was about as bad as most would have guessed for WSU’s defense, which had been mostly respectable against lesser offenses before meeting OSU’s, which ranks among the most productive in the nation. Atkinson entered the game leading the FBS in passing yards and TDs, and Legree was tops in the country in receiving yards. The Cougs can live with the fact that they only let Legree get loose for one big play downfield, but they’ll be kicking themselves for giving up so many chunk plays and such a high yardage total.

Tackling seemed to be an issue for WSU defenders. OSU averaged 6.3 yards per carry. Beavs running back AJ Newberry had three explosive runs, plus an 88-yard TD on a screen pass. No one was there to cover the play, and Newberry made the final WSU defender look silly with a juke and a hurdle.

WSU QB situation receives answer

Eshelman was called into action this week to replace struggling starter Caden Pinnick, and the redshirt freshman performed well considering the circumstances. He should be the Cougs’ signal-caller going forward.

Eshelman finished 32 of 49 for 289 yards – a season high in passing yards for WSU QBs – with two passing TDs and an interception (at the very end of the game). He showed savvy on run-pass options, rushing for 136 yards and a TD on 15 carries for the most productive rushing day by a WSU QB since John Mateer.

Eshelman’s performance was a positive for WSU’s offense.

Junior receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy was also a bright spot. He got open more than any WSU wideout has throughout the season, catching 11 passes for 147 yards and a 40-yard TD just before the half. Give some credit to coach/playcaller Kirby Moore for looking to stretch the field a bit more, though WSU connected on just three passes of 15-plus yards. The Cougars finished with 459 yards, their most in a game this season against an FBS opponent.

But there still were too many negatives. WSU tailbacks combined for 25 yards on 13 carries. Eshelman accounted for all six of WSU’s runs that gained 10-plus yards.

The Cougars went 7-for-17 on third downs – they were 0-for-9 on third-down tries before the fourth quarter, when they made the score look more respectable with a couple of TDs after going down 41-16.

WSU punted on its first four possessions, going three-and-out on three of those, allowing Oregon State to get off to a fast start and jump out to a 17-0 lead in the first quarter.

Another unfortunate note: WSU lost receiver Darrius Clemons to injury in the first half. He was on crutches after halftime. The Cougs are already down standout wideout Tony Freeman, who sustained a season-ending ACL injury in Week 1.

Beavs emerge as great story, Cougs still searching for identity

Seeing what the Beavers have become in Year 1 of the rebuilt Pac-12 is no doubt painful for WSU fans as their team has become irrelevant in 2026.

The teams had near-parallel paths to this point – left for dead after the Pac-12 imploded, playing through a couple of seasons without a conference home, going through coaching uncertainty, etc. Now, Oregon State is one of the best stories in the Group of Six, one of the best teams in the conference. The Cougars wish they were in their rivals’ shoes.

Sure, it would have been nice if both programs rose from the ashes as contenders in the new Pac-12. Unfortunately, only one has made the most of the situation thus far. The Beavers seemed to have picked a perfect fit as their new coach. They recruited the right transfer QB, a solid transfer running back and found a freshman gem at receiver. They created an identity and play with a style that’s entertaining and attracts attention.

Of course, it’s much too early to know if Moore was the right choice for WSU. He’ll get a grace period to build the program and to craft an identity. Pinnick seems to have been a miss, though. In any case, the Pac-12 legacy programs that have gone through the same struggles are facing opposite directions as of now. That can change. Hopefully, the Cougs/Beavs rivalry soon becomes one of the most competitive, anticipated G6 games of the year.

Washington State.title: Eshelman, Cougars hold their own in loss to Beavers | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
CORVALLIS, Ore. — There wasn’t much else Kirby Moore could do, not with the fireworks exploding, not with the fans erupting, not with the vaunted Oregon State passing attack torching Washington State defense and running away with the game before it could even get started.

So in the aftermath of the Beavers’ second long touchdown, an 88-yard score to follow their 90-yard strike in Saturday’s first half, Moore trotted his offense back on the field. The Cougars’ offense and quarterback Owen Eshelman, making his first career start, had to make up a two-score deficit before they got out of the first quarter.

WSU was already looking at a tall task, trying to upend OSU and its lively offense Saturday afternoon at Reser Stadium, but the visitors did themselves no favors in a 48-30 loss. In the first quarter, looking at two fourth-and-short situations near midfield, they elected to punt both times, and after each decision, the Beavers needed only one play to make them pay.

In short, that’s how Oregon State ran away with this victory, handing WSU (1-6, 0-3 Pac-12) its fourth straight loss in Eshelman’s first start at the college level. The Cougars, still looking for their first FBS victory in Moore’s debut season, gave up three quick scoring drives to open the game and couldn’t make up the ground.

About 18-point favorites heading into this one, the Beavers (4-2, 3-0) picked apart the Cougars for two long touchdowns, the first a 90-yard strike from quarterback Braden Atkinson to star freshman receiver Jesse Legree, the second an 88-yard connection from Atkinson to receiver AJ Newberry in the second frame. That score handed the hosts a 27-3 lead, which they had no problem maintaining the rest of the way.

For the game, Eshelman completed 32 of 49 passes for 257 yards, two touchdowns and one late interception — plus one rushing score — in his first start in place of Caden Pinnick, who started each of his team’s first six games. With a shade under two minutes to play, he lofted a deep touchdown pass to receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who finished with a career-best 147 yards on nine catches. And in the fourth, Eshelman lasered one to wideout Daniel Blood, who hauled in his first touchdown in the crimson and gray laundry.

Eshelman couldn’t produce a win in his first start, but all things considered, he looked sharp. He wasn’t afraid to let it fly, which Pinnick didn’t do much of in his tenure, and Eshelman didn’t commit any turnovers until a meaningless interception with the game out of reach in the fourth quarter, another weakness of Pinnick’s. As WSU prepares for its next game, a home matchup with first-place Boise State next weekend, the Cougars might feel encouraged about their offense. 

Eshelman also totaled 136 rushing yards, the most by a WSU quarterback since John Mateer in 2024, spotlighting an understated part of his game. He’s more of a pocket-passer than his predecessor, but Eshelman is plenty mobile, which he displayed on several occasions — including a 41-yard scamper early in the third frame.

In the first quarter, WSU receiver Darrius Clemons exited with what looked like a foot injury. After going to the locker room, he returned in warmup gear and sporting crutches. His outlook is unclear, but the Cougars have also been without star wideout Tony Freeman for almost the entire season, so any absence from Clemons would be bad news for Moore’s team.

All told, though, it was the best the Cougars’ offense has looked against an FBS opponent all season. They didn’t turn it over for the first time all season. Eshelman’s dual-threat abilities did wonders for WSU, even without left tackle Ashton Tripp, who missed the game with an ankle injury he sustained last weekend against Utah State. Washington transfer Maximus McCree stepped in in his place.

WSU also got a short rushing touchdown from quarterback Julian Dugger, who plunged in from three yards out, taking advantage of his athleticism. Dugger played a few scattered snaps in red-zone trips, underscoring the way coaches are trying to capitalize on his game.

But moving forward, the Cougs will have to shore up their defense, which was gashed by Atkinson, who completed 23 of 38 passes for 347 yards and three touchdowns. They became the latest victim of Legree, who racked up 108 receiving yards, clearing the century mark in all seven games of the season. Legree also scored on a five-yard reception midway through the third quarter.

Can WSU take down Boise State next weekend in Pullman? The Cougars will face long odds in that one, but they might be able to head into that one with something resembling momentum on offense, which they had not experienced much of earlier in the season.

Pregame

With its season spiraling, Washington State football turns to redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman to replace Caden Pinnick at quarterback.

Eshelman and the Cougars (1-5) travel to face fellow Pac-12 Conference holdover Oregon State (4-2) on the road.

Both teams are on opposite trajectories.

Washington State is still in search of its first FBS and conference win of the season. Meanwhile, after putting a scare into Houston and Texas Tech, Oregon State has won four games in a row and is tied with Boise State for first in the conference.

The Cougars’ defense, though stout, will have its work cut out for it against star freshman receiver Jesse Legree.

The game is scheduled to kick off at 3 p.m. on USA Network.

Series history

Washington State.title: Why Oregon State will beat Washington State | The pick
Washington State.summary:
PORTLAND – In his first season as Washington State’s defensive coordinator, Trent Bray has gotten just about as much as he can out of his group. The Cougars rank among the conference’s best defenses, and they’ve generated three interceptions, including two pick-sixes.

Plus, in WSU’s road game against Oregon State on Saturday afternoon, Bray will get a chance for a homecoming. An OSU alum and longtime coach, including head coach for roughly one and-a-half seasons, he’s quite familiar with the Beavers’ program.

But this WSU defense has never faced an offense quite like Oregon State’s, which is why we’re picking the Beavers to keep things rolling and hand the Cougars their fourth straight loss. OSU QB Braden Atkinson and star freshman wideout Jesse Legree still have not been slowed down, not even in their team’s two Power 4 losses to open the season, which is what makes this such a tall task for WSU.

Entering as 18.5-point underdogs, the Cougars might have a chance to pull an upset, thanks to head coach Kirby Moore’s decision to bench quarterback Caden Pinnick in favor of redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman, whose accuracy and big arm rank among his best traits. A lively offense might be what the Cougs have needed all along.

But that’s a lot to ask of a 20-year-old making his first career collegiate start, playing his first meaningful snaps at the college level. It’s hard to keep pace with this OSU offense, to match wits with the Beavers’ high-flying offense. There’s a reason why Atkinson leads the country with 376 passing yards per game.

WSU might not win Saturday’s game, but that doesn’t have to mean Moore’s decision to start Eshelman would be a mistake. The redshirt freshman could need some experience to settle into the role. Getting thrown into the fire in Corvallis would certainly help to that end. Final score: Oregon State 35, WSU 20

Washington State.title: WSU's keys to victory against Oregon State | Two-minute drill
Washington State.summary:
Washington State at Oregon State

Saturday, 3 p.m.

Line: Oregon State favored by 18½

TV: USA Network Radio: 920-AM

Key matchupWSU secondary against OSU receiver Jesse Legree: Nobody has the power to swing Saturday’s game quite like OSU freshman wideout Jesse Legree, who leads the country with 12 receiving touchdowns, winning Pac-12 Freshman of the Week honors all six weeks of the season thus far. He’s speedy and reliable, without a single drop on 54 targets. The Cougars’ secondary will have its hands full, particularly cornerbacks Jalil Tucker and Khamari Terrell, the latter of whom will likely get the Legree matchup.

Six teams have tried to slow quarterback Braden Atkinson, Legree and the Beavers’ offense. Six have failed. What does that mean for WSU’s chances on defense? To give themselves a shot, the Cougars’ pass-rushing duo of Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk will have to generate pressure on Atkinson. But OSU’s offensive line has been responsible for just two sacks.

To generate meaningful pass rush, the Cougars might target the two weak spots on the Beavs’ offensive line: right tackle Teko Shoats, who has been dinged for 10 pressures, according to Pro Football Focus; and right guard Tyler Voltin, who has given up two sacks. For WSU, that puts the onus on McLain and Zunk, plus interior linemen like Kaden Beatty and Jirah Leaupepetele, the latter of whom generated a solo sack last weekend against Utah State.

How the Cougs win…

To spring an upset, WSU would have to see one of two things happen: significantly limit Oregon State’s offense or get a big day from QB Owen Eshelman and the offense. If either happens, odds might skew the way of the Cougs’ offense, which has been rotten this season – but with Eshelman coming in for Caden Pinnick, whose turnovers and inability to stretch the field hampered his offense, the visitors might be able to surprise the Beavers.

If Eshelman can hit on a few passes early, it might open things up for WSU’s rushing game, which is still trying to break out in a consistent way. Tailbacks Maxwell Woods and Kirby Vorhees haven’t gotten many chances on the ground, much of that a credit to their offense’s bad habit of quick three-and-outs, but with enough carries, they might have a chance to keep their offense on the field.

How the Beavers win…

Oregon State can win this game the same way it has each of its last four: by unleashing a surging offense. Atkinson and Legree could be in for a big day against the WSU defense, whose one weakness has been giving up big plays, which accounted for one of the touchdowns Utah State used to beat the Cougars last weekend.

The Cougs have defended the run well, especially in short-yardage situations, but they’ve never done so against a passing offense as potent as the Beavs’. That could mean opportunities for OSU running backs AJ Newberry and Cornell Hatcher Jr., who have combined for 475 rushing yards and six scores on the ground.

Key stat: 0

That’s how many times Legree has been held to under 100 receiving yards this fall. It’s also the amount of times Atkinson has passed for fewer than 300 yards. WSU might be able to find a way to pull an upset while allowing those trends to continue, but it doesn’t look likely.

Quotable

“I want to win out,” WSU linebacker Keith Brown said. ” I think we have the talent to win out. I wanna do that. I wanna go out my senior year with multiple wins under our belt, and yeah, just continue to try and get better every single day and put our best foot forward.”

Washington State.title: To spring an upset on Oregon State, WSU and QB Owen Eshelman might have to keep pace on offense
Washington State.summary:
PORTLAND – When he thinks back, Keith Brown can still remember the first time he started a game at the college level. This was five years ago, Washington State’s veteran linebacker recalls, back when he was playing for Oregon and the Ducks walked into Columbus to take on a top-five Ohio State club.

A true freshman, Brown made two tackles in that game, helping his Ducks upset the third-ranked Buckeyes.

“You’re just kinda excited when it happens,” Brown said earlier this week. “At least for me, when it happened for me, I felt like I was so prepared for the game that I wasn’t nervous. Owen’s a true competitor. He’s very locked in, so I’m sure it’s the same for him.”

That would be redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman, who is taking over at quarterback for WSU, which is set to take on Oregon State at 3 p.m. Saturday on USA Network in Corvallis, where the Beavers opened as 17.5-point favorites. It’ll be the first start for Eshelman, who is taking over for signal-caller Caden Pinnick, whose struggles in the passing game contributed in a big way to the Cougars’ floundering offense.

To help WSU (1-5, 0-2 Pac-12) earn its first FBS win of the year and end a three-game slide, Eshelman and the Cougars’ offense will have to be much better than they have been all year. The Cougs are averaging just 12.6 points per game, which is just seven spots up from last in the country, and their minus-6 turnover margin ranks No. 129, meaning only four other teams in the nation have a worse mark.

Those are all key reasons why WSU coach Kirby Moore decided to bench Pinnick and pivot to Eshelman, who has played just two snaps in his college career, which came in garbage time against FCS Duquesne earlier this season. Listed at 6-foot-3 and 204 pounds, Eshelman’s best qualities center around his live arm and sharp accuracy, which could unlock a gear that WSU has yet to find in its offense.

A former three-star product of Norman North High in Oklahoma, Eshelman takes over at a tough spot for WSU. Off to their worst six-game start since 2010, the Cougars need a string of wins to save their bowl streak, which stands at 10 times in the last 11 full seasons. Moore has already made a couple changes to turn around this offense, including taking over playcalling duties ahead of his team’s previous game, a road loss to Utah State last weekend.

The only problem for the Cougars: They’re taking on a Beaver team that ranks among the hottest in the country. Thanks in large part to quarterback Braden Atkinson and freshman wideout Jesse Legree, Oregon State (4-2, 2-0) ranks fifth nationwide with 522 yards per game of total offense, coming off a 66-14 home dismantling of San Diego State. In short: The Beavs’ offense is electric, and the Cougs’ defense will get perhaps its tallest task of the season.

“He’s a really good player,” Moore said of Legree, who leads the country with 12 receiving touchdowns, including three apiece in his last two outings. “You see him with the ball in space, obviously taking the top off a number of times as well. I think it’s about playing team defense. Obviously, communication is gonna be really important: Where he’s at, whether he’s in the slot, whether he’s outside, left, right. The pass rush has to help out the coverage. The coverage has gotta help out the pass rush. I think Coach (Trent) Bray is doing a good job right now with our guys, making sure they’re all on the same page.”

It’s also a homecoming for Bray, an Oregon State alum who coached 11 years at his alma mater, including the full 2024 season and part of the 2025 campaign before being fired amid the Beavers’ 0-7 start to the season. In fact, the OSU connections on this WSU team number far more: Receiver Darrius Clemons and cornerback Jalil Tucker each transferred from Oregon State, true freshman Lance McGee was committed there before flipping to the Cougars and chief of staff Dan Van De Riet worked with the Beavers’ program in different capacities for 20 years.

Plus, this year, WSU and OSU won’t just be playing for bragging rights. The schools will also be playing for a new trophy, a new rivalry rock, which has yet to be named. The trophy isn’t official – it’s more of a fan and alumni-sponsored push than a school-sanctioned tradition – and the winner won’t hoist it at midfield like other trophies. But it does add a layer of intrigue to the WSU and OSU series, which will play installment No. 112 on Saturday afternoon.

“Hey,” Brown said earlier this week, “let’s go win the rock.”

To do that, the Cougars will have to find a way to slow down Atkinson and the Beavers’ offense, which nobody outside two Power 4 opponents have done so far. Atkinson, who ranks first nationwide with 376 passing yards per game, has tossed 21 touchdowns against just two interceptions. He’s thrown seven of his scores on deep passes, according to Pro Football Focus, highlighting the way he’s able to stretch the field.

It’s not exactly promising news for this WSU defense, which has played exceptionally well all season and kept the team in games, a remarkable feat in the face of the Cougs’ scuffling offense. But if the Cougars have shown one weakness on defense, it’s that they’re susceptible to allowing explosive plays, like a long touchdown pass against Utah State last weekend and a 75-yard touchdown rush against Kansas State last month.

Even if Bray and the Washington State defense can produce a few key stops, there’s also the matter of Eshelman and the WSU offense. Can the Cougs score enough to keep pace? In his first real college action, can Eshelman get it going through the air? Even if he throws an interception, though, his offense might be better for the bold approach. With Pinnick at the controls, WSU’s offense never looked capable of stretching the field.

Eshelman might have that capability. But it’s still a challenge for WSU, on both sides of the ball.

“There’s definitely some similarities in terms of playmaking ability,” Moore said, comparing Eshelman and Pinnick’s styles. “I think the big thing is we gotta continue to work on accuracy with the football, and when something’s there, we gotta take advantage of it and be more efficient on first and second down. Had opportunities there to drive in the red zone and didn’t take advantage of it, and then on third down, we gotta make sure we do a good job of taking care of the football. And sometimes it’s OK to punt. We’ve had some turnovers in those situations the last few games that have put our defense in bad positions.”

Washington State.title: 'Esh has that moxie': How WSU QB Owen Eshelman earned the chance to take over midseason
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Right away, coaches couldn’t help but notice the confidence, the poise that Owen Eshelman walked around with. He asked a slew of questions. He was involved in everything. He wanted to know the why behind calls and plays and formations.

This was in the spring of 2024, back when Eshelman was a high school junior, years away from landing at Washington State. He was on a visit to South Dakota State, where coaches were still evaluating him, making the 10-hour trek up from Oklahoma without even a scholarship offer in hand. As the Jackrabbits ran through a practice, a lively session only a few months after they had secured a second straight national championship, Eshelman wasn’t exactly standing off to the side.

Instead, Eshelman found his way to the Jackrabbits’ huddles, trying to learn the plays and get to know the players. He didn’t look overwhelmed the way many recruits on visits do, didn’t look anxious, wasn’t intimidated by the facility or coaches or tradition.

The impression that Eshelman made went more like this: Hey, I belong here. Even though I’m a 17-year-old on a visit, I’m gonna learn what these guys are doing at practice.

That was not lost on Danny Freund, then the Jackrabbits’ offensive coordinator, who was one of the lead recruiters on the lively-armed quarterback from central Oklahoma.

“He’s a guy in the locker room that everybody’s gonna play for because of the type of kid he is. So that’s one thing,” said Freund, who worked as WSU’s offensive coordinator last season, now with the same gig at North Dakota. “When I think about that position, you wanna have guys that the team is gonna play for, and you kinda have that it factor. Well, Esh has that moxie to him and that competitiveness and that personality, where I think guys will gravitate towards him.”

Two years and some change later, that’s one of the main reasons why Washington State is elevating Eshelman to the team’s starting quarterback role, putting trust in a redshirt freshman to try and revive a moribund offense. When Saturday afternoon arrives and WSU visits Oregon State, the Cougars’ quarterback won’t be Caden Pinnick, who started each of the team’s first six games. It will be Eshelman, who has just two snaps of college experience to his name.

Is Eshelman ready for such a task, to jump into the middle of the season and kickstart a rudderless WSU offense? We won’t know until 3 p.m. Saturday, when WSU matches wits with OSU, which boasts one of the country’s most electric offenses. Earlier this week, the Cougars (1-5, 0-2 Pac-12) decided to bench Pinnick, whose turnover problems were hampering his offense to the tune of just 12.6 points per game, opening the door for Eshelman and the live arm that made him such a captivating prospect out of Oklahoma.

Eshelman may not have much game experience, but a few things are clear about him. He’s listed at 6-foot-3 and 204 pounds, giving him solid size for the position. He might have the best arm in the Cougars’ quarterback room, which he showed off during the last two spring ball and fall camps, lasering the ball to all kinds of receivers. And while he’s closer to a pocket-passer than his predecessor, he’s plenty mobile too, quick to elude pressure and make plays on the run. He didn’t collect more than 1,300 rushing yards as a high school senior by accident.

There’s plenty more to Eshelman’s story, though: He hails from Norman, Oklahoma, where South Dakota State extended him his only offer out of Norman North High. He was planning to enroll at SDSU, but when former coach Jimmy Rogers left for the same job at WSU, Eshelman followed him there. Then last winter, when Rogers decamped for the job at Iowa State, Eshelman stayed put in Pullman.

That’s the short version of how Eshelman earned the opportunity to become the Cougars’ starting quarterback. To understand the full version, you have to understand Eshelman and his makeup, the traits that put him in that position to begin with.

“Owen’s one of the most competitive people I think I’ve ever been around, and he’s a great human being,” said Justin Jones, Eshelman’s head coach at Norman North. “Even as a young guy at 15, you could see the DNA there and what he was gonna bring to the table. Owen’s not gonna flinch. He’s very calm, cool and collected.”

• • •

The first time Eshelman played quarterback at the varsity level, he didn’t have to jump into action cold. He just had to move positions. One Friday night in the fall of 2022, Norman North was locked in a 6A playoff battle with Owasso, a perennial powerhouse in the classification. The Timberwolves were hanging around.

Then, in the second quarter, disaster struck: Quarterback Kamden Sixkiller, who would go on to land at McNeese State before transferring to Campbell, went down with an injury. It was devastating news for the Timberwolves, who had lost their first-team all-state pick. Who would fill in?

“I looked over the sidelines and told him he’s gotta go,” Jones said of Eshelman. “So he trotted out there and did it.”

At that point in the game, Eshelman was playing safety, where he had started each of the first 10 games of the season, playing with a physical approach. That helped him get identified by Chris Meyers, then the Jackrabbits’ recruiting coordinator, now at USC. Earlier that year, Norman North pulled off an upset of another powerhouse, Jenks, thanks to Eshelman’s game-sealing interception. “Esh was such a great athlete,” said Rocky Moore, the Timberwolves’ QB coach, “and just someone that you’re like, man, it would be a miss on our part as a staff if he wasn’t on the field in some capacity.”

All the same, Eshelman switched mid-game from safety to quarterback. By the time the game wrapped up, Eshelman had filled in admirably considering the circumstances, throwing for 303 yards and three touchdowns, plus two interceptions. Norman North fell in a one-score loss, ending the Timberwolves’ season, a disappointing ending to Eshelman’s first action at QB. But the tone was set: Eshelman had looked good, so good that coaches would make him Norman North’s full-time starter each of his final two seasons.

“We don’t win the game, but he gave us a chance,” Moore said, “and the kid didn’t blink.”

Which seems to beg the question: How? How does a teenager get thrown into the fire that way and perform so well? At the time, Eshelman was about 15 years old, still growing into the size that serves him so well now. What kind of 15-year-old can pull something like that off?

“The thing that keeps Esh ready is the way he prepares,” Moore said. “Whether he’s the starter or not, he’s gonna prepare himself that way. That’s just the way he was raised. That’s the standard that he lives by, and that’s not a cute piece for a story. That’s the truth about him.”

“His wiring has always been really helpful in that regard,” added Ryan Eshelman, Owen’s father. “I think even-keeled was a word that was used, not big swings in either direction, and so I think that confidence comes from preparation, and you just prepare and you prepare and you prepare, and that’s what enables you to step out and do your job in that regard.”

At every stop in his career, Eshelman’s preparation has struck everyone he’s been around, from his parents to his coaches, at Norman North and South Dakota State and WSU. Earlier this week, Cougar coach Kirby Moore noted that Eshelman’s preparation had always impressed him, that Eshelman’s work behind the scenes had helped him earn this opportunity. “He’s prepared like he’s the starter,” Moore said. Last year, Freund noticed the same, gushing about the results that could come “when you combine that work ethic with the talent that he has,” Freund said.

That year, Eshelman was a true freshman at WSU, not particularly close to seeing the field. He was one of five scholarship QBs on the team. He wasn’t traveling to road games, which is typical of signal-callers in his position. Eshelman’s talent was clear to anyone who had seen him play, but because of the natural progression of young quarterbacks at the college level, it wasn’t clear when he would get his shot.

Even in those days, Eshelman prepared like the day would come tomorrow. Coaches were surprised by his note-taking, the way he wrote everything down, in team meetings and position meetings and individual meetings. He steeped himself in details. He wanted an explanation behind everything, coaches said, but he wasn’t questioning authority. He just wanted to know the reason behind the names of playcalls, behind decisions of all kinds, so he could be as prepared as possible.

In those days, Eshelman was still raw, far more of an enticing prospect than a finished product. But the talent oozed out of him like sap off a maple tree. During fall camp last year, Freund remembers, former WSU quarterback Zevi Eckhaus took notice. “He would always say, ‘Esh is gonna be really good, bro. Like he’s gonna be really good.’ He just kinda knew,” Freund said. “That’s why I think everybody’s really excited about his potential.”

Rep by rep, Eshelman began to see the results. During this year’s spring practices and fall camp, Eshelman was squarely in the mix for the starting role, rotating in consistently for reps with the Cougars’ first-teamers. At one spring practice in Spokane, Eshelman unloaded a perfect fade pass to wideout Noah Westbrook, who hauled it in over his shoulder in the corner of the end zone. During one fall camp practice in August, he recorded one of his best throws as a Cougar, lofting a perfect deep pass to receiver Tony Freeman for a touchdown at Rogers Practice Field.

Eshelman wasn’t perfect, not by any stretch of the imagination. He missed throws and took avoidable sacks. Prepared as he was, he’s still a second-year freshman, and he made mistakes accordingly. In one fall camp scrimmage, he came inches away from throwing an interception. In Eshelman’s play, there was plenty of evidence that he was still learning the ropes of playing FBS football.

Still, two things were becoming clear. One: Eshelman had an enticing skillset, a booming arm and credible athleticism with his legs. Two: He was flourishing as a compelling leader, his teammates rallying around him with ease. His preparation was bleeding into his leadership, into his ability to keep his teammates pointed in the right direction, even as a redshirt freshman.

“Owen really took a good leadership role. He’s really vocal,” offensive lineman Ashton Tripp said after one fall camp practice. “So I’d say that’s a good positive.”

“Owen has a very steady demeanor. He doesn’t get too high, doesn’t get too low,” Moore said after a spring practice. “We always talk about emotional consistency. There’s a lot of highs and lows in athletics play-to-play, and I think that’s the demeanor that you have to have.”

“It’s real. It’s not fake with him,” Freund added. “It’s very, very genuine. As you guys start talking to him more, you’ll feel where there’s a natural leadership and instinct that he has. That was the biggest thing that we noticed in recruiting.”

Recruiting is what brought Eshelman from Norman to Pullman. But earlier this year, he was recruited once again, this time by a familiar face.

• • •

Last December, when Rogers decided to leave WSU for the same job at Iowa State, he upended just about everything with the Cougars’ program. He left them without a head coach, without two coordinators, without several star players who played key roles on that team: defenders Isaac Terrell and Bryson Lamb, Max Baloun and Sullivan Schlimgen.

As Rogers made the transition to Iowa State, he had to overhaul a roster, hitting the transfer portal to find players to plug holes. Former ISU signal-caller Rocco Becht had already followed coach Matt Campbell to Penn State, so Rogers needed a quarterback.

He reached out to Eshelman, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the situation, asking if he’d be interested in coming with him to Iowa State. Eshelman politely declined the opportunity, sources said.

“It stayed true to the kind of person he is,” Rocky Moore said.

The timeline of events, according to those in position to know, helped Eshelman decide to stay at WSU. Not long after taking the job at Iowa State, Rogers and his new staff began the process of filling out their roster, which means they made some of their moves within the first week or so.

Eshelman didn’t hear from ISU coaches until a bit later in that process, according to those sources. Plus, he was beginning to like what was going on in Pullman, where Moore had recently taken over and began filling out his staff and roster, doing so with an offensive-minded approach.

Iowa State got a commitment from its quarterback, Jaylen Raynor, on Jan. 3. Eshelman re-signed with WSU on the same day.

“Bigger and shinier wasn’t necessarily a selling point, you know?” Ryan said. “You see it all the time where somebody leaves to go somewhere else and it’s just not as good as what they left behind. So I think he just weighed it all and just felt like, ‘This feels like home, and I see a great future for me here.’ ”

• • •

There’s no use in sugarcoating it: There’s a bit of pressure on Eshelman this weekend. Washington State is known for producing prestigious quarterbacks, from Jack Thompson and Mark Rypien to Ryan Leaf to Drew Bledsoe, from Luke Falk and Gardner Minshew to Cam Ward and John Mateer. Who knows what the future holds, but in earning the Cougars’ QB1 designation, Eshelman takes the torch from those who laid the foundation.

Beyond all that, though, there’s the immediate. The Cougars could use a win this weekend to help turn their season around, to build some semblance of confidence in their fanbase, which has grown irritated with the way their team’s offense has floundered. Can Eshelman do his part to reverse that trend?

That’s a tale yet to be spun, but this won’t be the first time Eshelman has found himself in this kind of spot. Remember his first time playing the position at the high school level, when Norman North’s quarterback sustained an injury and prompted Eshelman to take his place? Four years later, he isn’t exactly taking over because of injury, but he is being asked to jump into action in a pinch.

To pull an upset on Oregon State, which opened as a 17.5-point favorite, Eshelman and the Cougars’ offense might have to score some points. The Beavers’ offense is one of the best in the country, spearheaded by quarterback Braden Atkinson and receiver Jesse Legree, and WSU will have to keep pace with that production.

To those who know him best, that’s where Eshelman’s preparation comes in handy. Before this opportunity came along, he wasn’t going through the motions with each passing game, knowing he wasn’t going to see the field. He was practicing like he would start the next game. Now he actually will.

It registers as a remarkable trait for a 20-year-old, a young man still learning how to navigate the world, much less an FBS football program. Is it a natural trait he has? Or a characteristic he learned from his parents?

“I think that may come the most natural for him,” said Libby Eshelman, Owen’s mother. “One of the things that we have worked to instill in our kids is where their identity comes from, and I think Owen has grabbed a hold of that. He loves football, and he does love to win. He loves the experience. But he knows at the end of the day, that does not define him, and I think that allows him to play more freely.”

“People are not always kind to quarterbacks, and so as a mom, I’m excited for him,” Libby added. “But I have some butterflies for him too.”

Nobody would fault Eshelman for having some, too. He’ll be prepared, though, the same way he was in previous games this fall. He wasn’t leading the huddle in those settings. He wasn’t leading that huddle at South Dakota State on his visit years ago, either, but he prepared like he was. Maybe his secret recipe was obvious all along.

Washington State.title: On Oregon State's rise, Washington State's fall and life on the edge in the sport's new era | Commentary
Washington State.summary:
They were together in the fight for survival, together in the salvage operation and together in the rebirth of Pac-12 football six weeks ago.

But when Oregon State and Washington State take the field Saturday afternoon in Corvallis, the connection won’t go much deeper than history and conference affiliation.

The Beavers are riveting, relevant and ascendant.

The Cougars are dull, immaterial and spiraling.

Their respective trajectories reflect life on the margins of major college football, where traditions are modest, resources limited and fates unpredictable.

Nobody expected the Beavers (4-2) to be one of the best stories in the sport under first-year coach JaMarcus Shephard, produce one of the game’s brightest young stars and emerge as a Pac-12 title contender with a path, albeit narrow, into the College Football Playoff.

Nobody expected the Cougars (1-5) to quickly sink to the bottom of the rebuilt conference under first-year coach Kirby Moore, with an inept offense, overburdened defense and the slimmest of chances to qualify for a bowl berth.

Washington State looks like a bad team in the new Pac-12.

Oregon State looks like a good team in the old Pac-12.

It’s easy enough to imagine alternate outcomes, with the Beavers flailing and the Cougars roaring.

The difference? A series of decisions made on each campus late last fall.

The Beavers had fired Trent Bray weeks earlier, following a dismal two-year stretch that coincided with the Pac-12’s transition period. The Cougars needed a coach after Jimmy Rogers bolted for Iowa State.

The schools took gigantic risks in handing the keys to rookie coaches. Neither spent much money. (Shephard and Moore are two of the lowest-paid coaches in the conference.) Both were desperate.

WSU wanted stability after churning through four coaches in seven years. OSU wanted energy and hope after slogging through the gloom of the Bray era. Both wanted leaders who could generate immediate success in the rebuilt conference.

How would success be defined? By three words: College Football Playoff.

Everything about the Pac-12, from the membership composition to the conference schedule to the resource allocation, was based on claiming the playoff berth reserved for the top team in the Group of Six.

Why? Because CFP appearances generate relevance and build brands and position schools outside the Big Ten and SEC for whatever comes next, whether it’s another round of realignment or a super league.

The sport’s status quo is unlikely to last into the 2030s. Every school in the ACC and Big 12 wants to jump into the Big Ten and SEC. Every school in the Pac-12 wants to move into the Big 12 and ACC.

The industry is hard-wired for ascent.

That’s why the Pac-12’s grant-of-rights contract binding the schools together expires in 2031.

That’s why WSU and OSU had to get their hires right.

The Cougars considered Bryan Harsin, the former Boise State coach, but are believed to have offered the job to Moore and nobody else. He was, it seems, their first choice.

The Beavers pursued North Dakota State’s Tim Polasek and Montana State’s Brent Vigen. Was Shephard the third choice? Only a handful of current and former school executives know, but he wasn’t the obvious first pick. That’s clear.

Sometimes, you get lucky. And when that luck combines with skill, breakthrough seasons follow.

Shephard has made all the right moves with staff and personnel decisions, particularly quarterback Braden Atkinson, a transfer from Mercer, and receiver Jesse Legree, a low-profile recruit from Baltimore.

He also hit with offensive coordinator Mitch Dalen, who learned his craft from Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer, and defensive playcaller Mike MacIntyre, a former national Coach of the Year (at Colorado).

And crucially, he hired a general manager, Eron Hodges, with an eye for roster construction.

Were the Cougars unlucky? Did they whiff with Moore? It’s too soon to declare a misfire.

But clearly, Moore has not made all the right decisions with his staff and roster. Last week, he stripped offensive coordinator Matt Miller of his playcalling duties. This week, Moore changed quarterbacks. If that doesn’t work, he’s out of options until December.

As currently constructed, the Cougars look overwhelmed, outmanned and out of their league – even though it is, in so many regards, their league.

They are winless against FBS competition and don’t appear capable of derailing the Beavers, who have won four consecutive games by an average of 36 points.

On the field, at least, WSU and OSU have gone their separate ways.

Their trajectories might cross again in one year, or in five. They could cross multiple times before the decade ends. On the sport’s margins, the only thing more fleeting than failure is success.

Washington State.title: Short fields and tough spots: WSU's defense has made the most of the circumstances
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN — In his long college football journey, Keith Brown has learned the importance of tuning out the noise. During Washington State’s fall camp, he deleted all social media off his phone, understanding that if he wants he and his unit to reach their potential, they can’t get sucked into the distractions.

Heck, he doesn’t always look at the scoreboard. Last month, in his WSU team’s home setback against Arizona, he went into halftime not knowing the score. He had to ask a teammate to find out, he said.

Turns out, that’s part of the reason how Brown and the Cougars have done their part on defense, using herculean efforts to keep their team in games when their floundering offense has left a lot out there. At least for Brown’s part, he’s done his best to ignore the problems his team’s offense is having, even if it means jogging out there for extra series thanks to turnovers.

“Just continue to compete,” Brown likes to tell his teammates.

As WSU defensive coordinator Trent Bray makes his return to Corvallis, where he worked as Oregon State’s head coach for the 2024 season and part of the 2025 campaign, the Cougars will have to do a lot of competing to pull an upset. The Beavers, who opened as 17.5-point favorites, own one of the country’s most prolific offenses, engineered in large part by quarterback Brayden Atkinson and true freshman wideout Jesse Legree.

Which leads to this question: How does WSU’s competitiveness on defense factor into a matchup with such a productive OSU offense?

“I don’t think it affects it at all. It’s just another opportunity to go out there and compete,” Brown said. “I’m sure our entire back end is just excited for the challenge, ready to do what they’re supposed to do. No matter who we’re playing, no matter what the rankings are and stuff like that, we always wanna go and play our best.”

As WSU’s offense earns all the headlines, turning things over to redshirt freshman quarterback Owen Eshelman over the struggling Caden Pinnick, perhaps a look at the Cougars’ defense is in order. Bray’s group has consistently held its own in the face of daunting circumstances, many of which have been caused by WSU’s offense, which has lost nine turnovers — seven from Pinnick.

First, consider this statistic, which paints the picture of what the Cougars’ defense is going through: In BCF Toys’ field position value rankings, WSU ranks dead last in the country, No. 138 of 138 FBS teams. In simplest terms, this means the Cougars are averaging the worst starting field position in the country, when averaging the drives their offense starts at the drives their defense starts at.

Whittle that down to just the starting field position WSU’s defense has averaged, though, and the problem becomes even clearer. The Cougars rank second-to-last nationally in that category, checking in with a mark of 65.2 — which means on average, opponents are starting drives at about their own 35-yard line. Only one other team, Rice, gives opponents better starting field position.

To be sure, though, this is not an indictment on WSU’s defense. It’s the opposite, an explanation behind some of the scores the Cougars have given up. In Washington State’s 17-16 loss to Utah State over the weekend, the visitors lost the lead in the fourth quarter, when a fumble from tight end Jack Pedersen set the Aggies up at the Cougar 19. Three plays later, they jogged into the end zone to take the lead for good.

That reality is best illustrated by BCF Toys’ defensive short field rankings, which measure how often a defense has to jog out with the opponent starting at its own 40 yard line or further. The Cougars’ defense has been handed those situations 25% of the time. Only 15 other defenses have met that fate more often.

All of that, though, only serves to make this WSU defense’s accomplishments even more impressive. In Friday’s game, defensive end Linus Zunk and defensive tackle Jirah Leaupepetele each earned sacks. The Cougs forced seven punts. On the season, they’ve forced five turnovers, about middle of the pack nationwide.

In six games, WSU is allowing 23.7 points per game, which is fifth in the Pac-12. Maybe that doesn’t sound very impressive — but then you consider what this group has been up against. That’s when their outings click, the genius behind Bray’s operation zooms into focus.

“We’re a very connected team,” Brown said. “We have our captains group chats, leadership meetings and stuff like that, and we just continue to reiterate that we’re a team at the end of the day. The last thing you wanna do is divide the team. There is no division. We’re one team. I think honestly, we’re just as close as we were going into week one. So I’m still excited for rest of the season.”
